lessons.title: Propositional logic and proof
lessons.prerequisite: Comfort with true/false statements and basic algebra.
lessons.intuition: A proposition has a definite truth value. Logic asks whether the structure of an argument is valid, independently of the subject matter. First translate sentences into symbols; then reason about all possible assignments, not just one convenient example.

sections.title: Connectives and implication
sections.body: AND is true only when both operands are true; OR is inclusive and false only when both are false. Negation reverses the truth value. P→Q is equivalent to ¬P∨Q: the promise fails only when P is true and Q is false. P↔Q requires equal truth values. XOR requires unequal values.

sections.title: Equivalence and normal forms
sections.body: Two expressions are equivalent if their truth-table columns match for every assignment. De Morgan’s laws change ¬(P∧Q) to ¬P∨¬Q and ¬(P∨Q) to ¬P∧¬Q. Distribute AND over OR to obtain disjunctive normal form, or OR over AND for conjunctive normal form. A tautology is always true; a contradiction is always false; a satisfiable expression is true for at least one assignment.

sections.title: Checking an argument
sections.body: An argument with premises A₁,…,Aₖ and conclusion C is valid if (A₁∧…∧Aₖ)→C is a tautology. To refute validity, find an assignment making all premises true and the conclusion false. The contrapositive ¬Q→¬P is equivalent to P→Q; the converse Q→P is not generally equivalent.

sections.title: Necessary versus sufficient: translating words
sections.body: “P only if Q” means that whenever P holds, Q must hold: P→Q. “P if Q” means Q is enough to establish P: Q→P. For example, “a number is divisible by 4 only if it is even” states divisibility by 4 implies evenness; the reverse is refuted by 6. A necessary condition can hold even when the target property does not. To test a proposed equivalence, translate each direction separately and look for a counterexample. In proofs, modus ponens uses P and P→Q to infer Q, while modus tollens uses ¬Q and P→Q to infer ¬P. Inferring P merely from Q is the invalid pattern called affirming the consequent.

examples.prompt: Show why P→Q and its converse differ
steps: Choose P=false and Q=true.
P→Q is true because its antecedent is false.
Q→P is false because its antecedent is true and consequent false. A single counterexample disproves equivalence.
Assume all premises true and try to make P→R false: P=true, R=false.
P→Q forces Q=true.
Q→R then forces R=true, a contradiction. No counterexample exists; the argument is valid.

pitfalls: Necessary and sufficient are directional: P sufficient for Q means P→Q.
“Only if Q” introduces Q as a necessary condition.
A true implication does not mean both P and Q are true.
revision: Contrapositive preserves meaning; converse need not.

checks.prompt: Which statement is equivalent to P→Q?
checks.hint: Think about the contrapositive.
checks.explanation: The contrapositive preserves the implication: ¬Q→¬P is equivalent to P→Q. Reversing alone gives the converse, which is not equivalent.

checks.prompt: For how many assignments to P,Q is P→Q true?
checks.hint: Identify its sole false case.
checks.explanation: TT, FT and FF make the implication true. TF makes it false, so 3 assignments work.

lessons.title: First-order logic and quantifiers
lessons.prerequisite: Propositional logic; understand a variable and a set.
lessons.intuition: A predicate becomes a proposition when its variables are given values or bound by quantifiers. The domain matters: “every number has a multiplicative inverse” changes truth when zero is included. Quantifier order expresses who gets to choose a value first.

sections.title: Meaning and scope
sections.body: ∀x P(x) requires P for every domain element; ∃x P(x) requires at least one witness. A bound variable lies within a quantifier’s scope; a free variable remains unspecified. Write brackets to show scope. “Every student knows some language” is ∀s ∃l Knows(s,l); it does not promise the same language for everyone.

sections.title: Negation
sections.body: Negating ∀ changes it to ∃ and negates the predicate: ¬∀x P(x) ≡ ∃x ¬P(x). Similarly ¬∃x P(x) ≡ ∀x ¬P(x). For multiple quantifiers apply this from the outside inward. Negating a conjunction or implication inside the predicate still requires propositional rules.

sections.title: Order and witnesses
sections.body: ∃y∀x R(x,y) selects one y that works for all x. ∀x∃y R(x,y) permits y to depend on x. The former implies the latter on the usual nonempty domains, but not conversely. To disprove a universal statement provide a counterexample; to prove an existential statement provide a witness.

sections.title: Choosing witnesses and refuting nested statements
sections.body: For ∀x∃y R(x,y), an explicit witness formula y=g(x) can prove the claim. To refute it, find one x for which every possible y fails. For ∃y∀x R(x,y), the witness must be chosen independently of x; refuting it requires showing that each candidate y fails for some x. Over integers, ∀x∃y(y>x) is true with y=x+1, but ∃y∀x(y>x) is false because for any proposed y, choosing x=y violates strict inequality. These are different orders of dependency, not different spellings of the same statement. When translating “only students passed,” write Passed(x)→Student(x); it does not assert that all students passed.

examples.prompt: Negate “every student passed at least one exam”
steps: Formalize as ∀s∃e Passed(s,e).
Move the negation inward: ∃s∀e ¬Passed(s,e).
Meaning: there is a student who passed no exams, not merely a student who failed one.

examples.prompt: Compare quantifiers for x+y=0 over integers
steps: For ∀x∃y, choose y=−x. This works for every x.
For ∃y∀x, a single fixed y would need to equal −x for all integers.
Taking x=0 and x=1 demands y=0 and y=−1 simultaneously; the second statement is false.

pitfalls: Changing quantifier order changes meaning.
Negation must reach the predicate, not stop at swapping symbols.
revision: State the domain before choosing witnesses.

checks.prompt: What is the negation of ∀x∃y R(x,y)?
checks.hint: Swap each quantifier while moving negation inward.
checks.explanation: ¬∀x∃y R = ∃x¬∃y R = ∃x∀y¬R. One x defeats every candidate y.

checks.prompt: For x,y in {0,1}, how many fixed values of y make ∀x: x+y=1 true?
checks.hint: One y must work for both choices of x.
checks.explanation: x=0 requires y=1 and x=1 requires y=0. No fixed y works.

lessons.title: Sets, relations and functions
lessons.intuition: Sets describe collections, relations describe permitted pairs, and functions choose one output for every input. Keep those three objects separate: a function is a special relation, but a general relation may connect an element to many others or none.

sections.title: Sets and counting
sections.body: A∪B includes elements in either set; A∩B includes elements in both; A−B removes B from A. A power set contains every subset, so |P(A)|=2^|A|. The Cartesian product A×B consists of ordered pairs and has |A|×|B| elements for finite sets. Inclusion–exclusion gives |A∪B|=|A|+|B|−|A∩B|.

sections.title: Properties of relations
sections.body: On A, reflexivity means aRa for every a. Symmetry means aRb implies bRa. Antisymmetry means aRb and bRa imply a=b. Transitivity means aRb and bRc imply aRc. Reflexive+symmetric+transitive defines an equivalence relation, whose equivalence classes partition A. Test the properties individually; loops and pair direction matter.

sections.title: Functions and inverses
sections.body: A function A→B is total and single-valued. Injectivity forbids two distinct inputs sharing an output; surjectivity requires every codomain element to be reached. Bijectivity combines both and permits a two-sided inverse. On finite sets of equal size, injectivity and surjectivity are equivalent; that shortcut depends on finiteness and equal cardinality.

sections.title: Relation matrices and composition
sections.body: For a finite set {a₁,…,aₙ}, represent a relation by a Boolean matrix M where Mᵢⱼ=1 iff aᵢRaⱼ. Reflexivity requires diagonal 1s; symmetry requires M=Mᵀ; antisymmetry disallows simultaneous off-diagonal 1s in symmetric positions. Transitivity requires that every two-edge path implies its direct relation pair. Relation composition uses Boolean matrix multiplication, where products use AND and sums use OR. The transitive closure adds all pairs reachable by paths, and need not add loops unless a path or reflexive closure requires them. For function composition g∘f, apply f first and then g; the right-hand function acts first. If both functions are injective, their composition is injective, but properties of a composition do not freely imply every property of each component.

steps: aRb iff 3 divides a−b. a−a=0 establishes reflexivity.
Reversing a−b changes its sign, preserving divisibility; adding two divisible differences establishes transitivity.
The classes are residues 0,1,2, so the relation is an equivalence relation.

examples.prompt: Count functions from a 3-element set to a 2-element set
steps: Each input independently selects one of two outputs: 2³=8 total functions.
A nonsurjective function uses only one output; there are two constant functions.
Thus 8−2=6 functions are surjective. None is injective, by the pigeonhole principle.

pitfalls: Antisymmetric does not mean “not symmetric”; identity relations satisfy both.
The codomain is part of a function definition; changing it can change surjectivity.
revision: Number of functions from m inputs to n outputs is nᵐ.
Equivalence classes are disjoint and cover the underlying set.

checks.prompt: Which properties define an equivalence relation?
checks.hint: Equivalence classes partition the set.
checks.explanation: Reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity define equivalence. Replacing symmetry with antisymmetry defines a partial order instead.

checks.prompt: How many functions exist from a 2-element set to a 3-element set?
checks.hint: Choose an output independently for each input.
checks.explanation: 3 choices for the first input times 3 for the second gives 9.

lessons.title: Partial orders and lattices
lessons.intuition: An order need not compare every pair. A dependency graph of tasks can say one task comes before another while leaving independent tasks incomparable. A lattice adds a reliable way to combine any two elements using their closest common upper and lower bounds.

sections.title: Partial order and diagrams
sections.body: A partial order is reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive. If every pair is comparable, it is a total order. A Hasse diagram omits loops and edges implied by transitivity; lower-to-higher paths imply the order. An edge represents a cover relation: no element lies strictly between its endpoints.

sections.title: Extremal elements
sections.body: A least element is below every element and is unique if it exists; a minimal element has no strictly smaller element and several may exist. Greatest and maximal are dual. An upper bound of a pair lies above both; the least upper bound is the smallest among those bounds, not just any convenient upper bound.

sections.title: Lattice operations
sections.body: A lattice requires every pair to have a unique least upper bound (join) and greatest lower bound (meet). In a power-set lattice ordered by inclusion, join is union and meet is intersection. For positive divisors of an integer ordered by divisibility, join is lcm and meet is gcd. A finite lattice has top and bottom elements.

sections.title: Finding bounds without confusing numeric order
sections.body: To find an upper bound of a,b in an arbitrary poset, list elements x for which a≤x and b≤x according to the defined relation. Among these candidates, a least upper bound must be below every other upper bound. A merely minimal upper bound might fail that requirement; two incomparable minimal upper bounds mean there is no join. For a Hasse diagram, follow upward paths from both elements and intersect their reachable sets. Repeat downward for lower bounds. In a finite poset, having a top and bottom alone does not make it a lattice: the pairwise meet and join requirement still needs checking. In subset inclusion, these constructions reduce to union and intersection because those sets satisfy the universal bound definitions.

examples.prompt: Find meet and join of 4 and 6 among divisors of 12
steps: Common divisors are 1 and 2; the greatest under divisibility is 2.
Common multiples inside the set include 12; lcm(4,6)=12.
Thus meet=2 and join=12. Numerical minimum and maximum would have given the wrong answer.

examples.prompt: Identify minimal versus least in {2,3,6}, ordered by divisibility
steps: 2 and 3 have no smaller element in the set, so both are minimal.
Neither divides the other, so neither is below every element.
There is no least element; 6 is greatest because both 2 and 3 divide it.

pitfalls: Do not draw all transitive edges in a Hasse diagram.
Minimal does not imply least.
revision: Join is least upper bound; meet is greatest lower bound.

checks.prompt: Which condition is required for a poset to be a lattice?
checks.hint: The requirement concerns pairwise bounds.
checks.explanation: Every pair needs a greatest lower bound and a least upper bound. Total comparability is unnecessary; a subset-inclusion lattice can have incomparable elements.
options: It has at least one minimal element
Every pair has a meet and a join

checks.prompt: How many elements are in the power-set lattice of a 3-element set?
checks.hint: All subsets are nodes.
checks.explanation: There are 2³=8 subsets.

lessons.title: Monoids and groups
lessons.intuition: An algebraic structure is a set together with an operation and laws. Start with closure: combining allowed objects must produce another allowed object. Additional laws let you reorganize computations, introduce an empty operation, or undo an operation.

sections.title: Semigroup and monoid
sections.body: A binary operation maps S×S into S. Associativity says (a*b)*c=a*(b*c) and permits dropping parentheses. A semigroup is closed and associative. A monoid additionally has an identity e with e*a=a*e=a. Strings under concatenation form a monoid; the empty string is the identity. Concatenation is generally not commutative.

sections.title: Group axioms
sections.body: A group is a monoid in which every element a has an inverse a⁻¹ satisfying a*a⁻¹=a⁻¹*a=e. Commutativity is not required; when it holds, the group is abelian. Integers under addition form an abelian group; nonnegative integers under addition form only a monoid because positive values have no additive inverse there.

sections.title: Modular examples and uniqueness
sections.body: Residues modulo n under addition form a group with identity 0 and inverse n−a modulo n. Under multiplication, only residues relatively prime to n have modular inverses. Identities and inverses are unique in a group: apply the identity laws or associativity to show any two candidates must coincide.

sections.title: Cancellation and element order
sections.body: Group inverses justify cancellation: from a*b=a*c, multiply on the left by a⁻¹ and use associativity to obtain b=c. A general monoid need not permit this. The order of a group element is the least positive k for which aᵏ=e, if such a k exists; this means repeated application of the group operation, so under addition use repeated sums. In addition modulo 6, element 2 has order 3 because 2+2+2≡0, while neither one nor two repetitions is zero. For a finite group, the order of an element divides group size by Lagrange’s theorem. The theorem gives a necessary divisibility condition, not a guarantee that every divisor is realized by an element in every group.

examples.prompt: Is multiplication on {1,2,3,4} modulo 5 a group?
steps: Products of nonzero residues remain nonzero modulo prime 5; associativity is inherited.
Identity is 1; inverses are 1↔1, 2↔3, 4↔4.
All axioms hold, and multiplication is commutative, so it is an abelian group.

examples.prompt: Find the additive inverse of 5 modulo 8
steps: We need 5+x ≡ 0 mod 8.
The identity is 0, not 1, because the operation is addition.

pitfalls: Always specify both the set and operation.
A multiplicative inverse modulo composite n does not exist for every nonzero residue.
revision: Group = monoid + inverse for every element.

checks.prompt: Nonnegative integers under addition form which structure?
checks.hint: Ask whether positive elements have inverses inside the set.
checks.explanation: Addition is closed and associative with identity 0. Positive integers have no additive inverse among nonnegative integers, so this is not a group.
options: Monoid with identity 0, but not a group

checks.prompt: What is the multiplicative inverse of 3 modulo 7, expressed between 0 and 6?
checks.hint: Solve 3x ≡ 1 mod 7.

lessons.title: Graph connectivity, matching and colouring
lessons.intuition: Graphs model pairwise connections. Connectivity is about reachability, matching allocates disjoint pairs, and colouring separates conflicting neighbours. A question can involve the same drawing but demand a completely different invariant, so identify the task before computing.

sections.title: Degrees and connectivity
sections.body: For an undirected graph, the sum of vertex degrees is 2E because every edge has two endpoints. A path joins vertices; connected components are maximal connected regions. A connected acyclic undirected graph is a tree with V−1 edges. Removing a bridge increases component count; removing an articulation vertex can disconnect the graph.

sections.title: Matching
sections.body: A matching is a set of edges sharing no endpoints. A maximum matching has the largest cardinality; a maximal matching merely cannot be enlarged by adding an edge. In a bipartite graph with parts X,Y, Hall’s theorem gives a matching saturating X iff every subset S of X satisfies |N(S)|≥|S|. Check deficient subsets rather than just individual degrees.

sections.title: Colouring
sections.body: A proper vertex colouring assigns different colours to adjacent vertices. The minimum number is the chromatic number. A complete graph Kₙ needs n colours. A graph is bipartite iff it has no odd cycle; any nonempty bipartite graph with an edge needs two colours. Colouring disconnected components can reuse colours.

sections.title: Chromatic bounds and matching certificates
sections.body: A clique of size k forces at least k vertex colours because every pair in it is adjacent. Conversely a greedy colouring uses at most Δ+1 colours, where Δ is maximum degree: when colouring a vertex, at most Δ neighbour colours can be forbidden. These are bounds, not generally equal values. For a path with at least one edge, alternating two colours proves χ=2. A matching can be improved along an augmenting path whose edges alternate unmatched and matched, beginning and ending at unmatched vertices. Flipping membership along that path increases matching size by one. An absent augmenting path certifies maximum matching under the standard matching theorem; merely being unable to add a single isolated edge certifies only maximality.

steps: Five vertices each have degree 2, so the degree sum is 10 and there are 5 edges.
The largest matching has floor(5/2)=2 edges because each edge consumes two vertices; such a matching exists.
An odd cycle is not bipartite and needs 3 colours; alternating two colours fails at the closing edge.
Let X={a,b,c}, Y={1,2,3}; a and b connect only to 1, while c connects to 2 and 3.
For S={a,b}, the neighbour set has only one element.
|N(S)|=1<2 proves there is no matching saturating X, even though every vertex of X has a neighbour.

pitfalls: Maximal and maximum are different optimization concepts.
A directed graph requires specifying weak or strong connectivity.

checks.prompt: Which statement distinguishes maximal and maximum matchings?
checks.hint: Local inability to add an edge need not prove global optimality.
checks.explanation: Maximum optimizes cardinality over all matchings. Maximal only forbids adding an edge to the current set; rearranging chosen edges may yield a larger matching.
options: They always mean the same thing
Maximum means largest cardinality; maximal means no edge can simply be added
Maximum matchings can be enlarged by adding an edge

lessons.intuition: Counting is most reliable when you describe a construction of the object. Ask whether order matters, repetition is allowed, and restrictions are independent. Formulas follow those choices; picking a formula before interpreting the object is a common source of errors.

sections.title: Sum and product rules
sections.body: Use addition for disjoint alternative cases and multiplication for successive independent choices. Ordered selections without replacement are n!/(n−r)!; unordered selections divide by r!, giving C(n,r). If ordered positions can repeat symbols from an alphabet of size n, there are nʳ assignments.

sections.title: Restrictions and overcounting
sections.body: For at least one occurrence, count all objects minus those with none. Inclusion–exclusion adds single-set counts, subtracts pair overlaps, and adds triple overlaps. Stars and bars counts nonnegative integer solutions x₁+…+xₖ=n as C(n+k−1,k−1); for positive solutions first subtract one from each variable.

sections.title: Pigeonhole reasoning
sections.body: Putting more than k objects into k boxes forces some box to contain at least two. The generalized bound is at least ceiling(n/k) objects in one box. Define the boxes clearly: residues modulo an integer, months, or possible degree values. The principle guarantees existence but usually does not identify the object.

sections.title: Inclusion–exclusion with three sets
sections.body: For three events or finite sets, |A∪B∪C|=|A|+|B|+|C|−|A∩B|−|A∩C|−|B∩C|+|A∩B∩C|. An element in all three was initially counted three times, then subtracted three times, so it needs adding once. This accounting explains the signs rather than just memorizing them. To count positive solutions to x+y+z=7, set u=x−1,v=y−1,w=z−1. Then u+v+w=4 with nonnegative variables, so there are C(6,2)=15 solutions. Pigeonhole statements also need tight boxes: among 13 people, two share a birth month, but this does not mean exactly two do or identify which month.

pitfalls: Divide by r! only when every unordered object was counted exactly r! times.
At least and exactly require different case logic.

lessons.title: Recurrence relations and generating functions
lessons.intuition: A recurrence expresses a large object in terms of smaller ones, but base cases determine which sequence it describes. A generating function turns an entire sequence into one formal algebraic object; coefficients store the answers while multiplication represents convolution.

sections.title: Solving recurrences
sections.body: First compute a few terms and record initial values. For aₙ=c aₙ₋₁, repeated substitution gives aₙ=cⁿa₀. For aₙ=r aₙ₋₁+b, expand a geometric sum. Linear homogeneous recurrences with constant coefficients use characteristic roots: aₙ=u aₙ₋₁+v aₙ₋₂ yields λ²−uλ−v=0. Distinct roots give Aλ₁ⁿ+Bλ₂ⁿ; repeated roots need a factor n.

sections.title: Generating-function identities
sections.body: Define A(x)=Σₙ≥₀ aₙxⁿ. The constant sequence 1 has generating function 1/(1−x). Differentiate the geometric series formally to obtain Σnxⁿ=x/(1−x)². An index shift requires accounting for omitted initial terms: Σₙ≥₁aₙ₋₁xⁿ=xA(x).

sections.title: Derivation from a recurrence
sections.body: Multiply both sides by xⁿ and sum over the indices for which the recurrence holds. Isolate A(x), keeping boundary terms. Expand the resulting rational function or use known identities to recover coefficients. This method also models counting when choices concatenate and coefficient sums represent total size.

sections.title: Characteristic-root derivation
sections.body: For aₙ=3aₙ₋₁−2aₙ₋₂, try a solution λⁿ. Substitution and division by λⁿ⁻² gives λ²−3λ+2=0, whose roots are 1 and 2. Therefore aₙ=A+B2ⁿ for distinct roots. With a₀=0,a₁=1, solve A+B=0 and A+2B=1 to obtain B=1,A=−1, hence aₙ=2ⁿ−1. Initial values select the constants; the recurrence alone specifies many possible sequences. With a repeated root λ, the independent solutions include λⁿ and nλⁿ. A nonhomogeneous recurrence needs a particular solution in addition to homogeneous solutions; a trial form overlapping the homogeneous solution may require multiplication by n.

steps: Expand: aₙ=2(2aₙ₋₂+1)+1=4aₙ₋₂+3.
Continuing gives aₙ=2ⁿa₀+Σᵢ₌₀ⁿ⁻¹2ⁱ.
The geometric sum is 2ⁿ−1, so aₙ=2ⁿ−1; check a₁=1 and a₂=3.

steps: Split the sum into 2Σnxⁿ+3Σxⁿ.
Substitute identities: 2x/(1−x)²+3/(1−x).
Use a common denominator to obtain (3−x)/(1−x)².

pitfalls: Never drop initial values when shifting an index.
A repeated characteristic root needs an extra n factor.
revision: Check any closed form against base cases.

lessons.title: Matrices, determinants and linear systems
lessons.intuition: A matrix is a compact representation of a linear transformation or system. Row reduction exposes independent constraints. Rank counts independent directions, not the number of rows; redundant equations cannot determine additional unknowns.

sections.title: Matrix operations and determinants
sections.body: An m×n matrix multiplies an n×p matrix to give m×p; multiplication is generally noncommutative. For a 2×2 matrix [[a,b],[c,d]], det=ad−bc. Swapping rows reverses determinant sign; scaling a row scales determinant; adding a multiple of another row leaves it unchanged. A square matrix is invertible iff its determinant is nonzero.

sections.title: Elimination and rank
sections.body: Gaussian elimination uses elementary row operations to form echelon shape. Each pivot corresponds to an independent row and column direction; rank is the number of pivots. A zero row in the coefficient matrix may simply be redundancy, while a row [0 … 0 | nonzero] in the augmented matrix is a contradiction.

sections.title: Classifying solutions
sections.body: For Ax=b, consistency requires rank(A)=rank([A|b]). If consistent and rank(A)=n unknowns, the solution is unique. If rank<n, there are n−rank free variables and infinitely many real solutions. The homogeneous system Ax=0 is always consistent and has nonzero solutions exactly when rank<n.

sections.title: Elimination as a reproducible procedure
sections.body: Choose a nonzero pivot in the current column, swap a row into the pivot position if needed, and eliminate entries below it. Move to the next pivot row and later column, skipping columns that cannot supply a pivot. Row operations must apply to the augmented right-hand side as well as coefficients. For x+y=3 and x−y=1, subtract the second equation from the first to obtain 2y=2, so y=1 and x=2. To find an inverse, augment A with I and row-reduce [A|I] to [I|A⁻¹]. Failure to reach a pivot in each column of square A proves singularity. Determinant changes must be tracked if using elimination to compute det(A).

The inverse is (−1/2)[[4,−2],[−3,1]]; multiplying verifies identity.

pitfalls: Count pivots rather than nonzero-looking original rows.
An inconsistent augmented row is not the same as a redundant zero row.

lessons.title: Eigenvalues, eigenvectors and LU decomposition
lessons.intuition: An eigenvector is a direction a linear transformation stretches without rotating it away from that line. LU decomposition instead records the elimination process so many systems sharing the same coefficient matrix can be solved cheaply.

sections.title: Finding eigenspaces
sections.body: Av=λv means (A−λI)v=0 with v≠0. A nonzero solution requires det(A−λI)=0, the characteristic equation. For each root λ, row-reduce A−λI to find its nullspace. Eigenvectors can be scaled by nonzero constants; zero is never an eigenvector.

sections.title: Useful checks and diagonalization
sections.body: The eigenvalue sum equals trace and product equals determinant, counting algebraic multiplicity. Triangular matrices have diagonal entries as eigenvalues. A matrix is diagonalizable if it has enough linearly independent eigenvectors. A repeated eigenvalue does not alone prevent diagonalization, but its eigenspace may be too small.

sections.title: LU solving
sections.body: Gaussian elimination can factor A=LU, with L lower triangular and U upper triangular. Multipliers are stored in L. Solve Ly=b by forward substitution and Ux=y by backward substitution. If elimination needs row swaps, use a permutation matrix: PA=LU. Factor once, then solve repeated right-hand sides without repeating elimination.

sections.title: Repeated eigenvalues and independent directions
sections.body: The matrix [[2,1],[0,2]] has characteristic polynomial (2−λ)², but solving (A−2I)v=0 forces v₂=0. Its eigenspace has dimension one, so two independent eigenvectors do not exist and the matrix is not diagonalizable. By contrast 2I has the same repeated eigenvalue but every nonzero vector is an eigenvector, giving a two-dimensional eigenspace. Algebraic multiplicity counts characteristic roots; geometric multiplicity is nullity of A−λI. The geometric multiplicity cannot exceed algebraic multiplicity. For repeated linear solves using LU, factorization costs roughly cubic work for dense matrices while each triangular solve costs quadratic work, explaining why reusing factors is beneficial.

steps: The characteristic determinant is (2−λ)(3−λ).
Roots are 2 and 3, matching the diagonal entries.
For λ=2, v₂=0; for λ=3, v₂=v₁. Directions (1,0) and (1,1) are independent.
Eliminate the 4 using multiplier 4/2=2: second row minus twice first gives [0,1].
Multiplying LU gives [[2,1],[4,3]], confirming the factorization.

pitfalls: An eigenvalue of zero implies singularity, but zero is not an eigenvector.
Do not ignore permutation matrices when a pivot is zero.

checks.hint: Compare 2I with a Jordan-block example.
checks.explanation: A repeated eigenvalue may or may not have enough independent eigenvectors. Geometric multiplicity determines the available directions.

lessons.title: Limits, continuity and differentiability
lessons.intuition: A limit describes nearby behaviour, while a function value describes the point itself. Continuity joins those ideas. Differentiability asks for one consistent local slope, a stronger requirement than having no break in the graph.

sections.title: Evaluating limits
sections.body: A two-sided limit exists when left and right limits agree. Try substitution first; an indeterminate 0/0 asks for simplification, not an answer. Factor and cancel on a punctured neighbourhood, rationalize radicals, or use standard limits such as sin x/x→1 in radians. Cancellation does not redefine the function at the removed point.

sections.title: Continuity
sections.body: At a, require f(a) to be defined, limₓ→ₐf(x) to exist, and both to agree. For piecewise functions check both sides and the assigned point value. A removable discontinuity can be repaired by defining the missing value to equal the limit; jump discontinuities cannot be repaired by one point assignment.

sections.title: Derivative from definition
sections.body: f′(a)=limₕ→₀[f(a+h)−f(a)]/h. Left and right derivative limits must agree. Differentiability implies continuity because the increment equals h times a bounded difference quotient near the point. Continuity does not imply differentiability: a corner can have conflicting one-sided slopes.

sections.title: Piecewise continuity and matching slopes
sections.body: Consider f(x)=ax+b for x<1 and f(x)=x² for x≥1. Right-side value and limit at 1 are both 1. Continuity requires a+b=1. The left derivative is a while the right derivative is 2, so differentiability additionally requires a=2, hence b=−1. Matching values alone leaves many continuous choices, but only the matching slope gives differentiability here. For limits involving infinity, divide polynomial numerator and denominator by their highest relevant power of x to compare growth. A limit can exist even when the function is undefined at the point. Neither observing a plot nor substituting a few nearby values proves the exact limiting behaviour.

steps: Direct substitution gives 0/0, so factor x²−4=(x−2)(x+2).
For x≠2 the quotient equals x+2.
Its limit is 4. The original function remains undefined at 2 unless explicitly extended.
The function approaches zero from both sides and equals zero, so it is continuous.
For h>0, |h|/h=1; for h<0, it equals −1.
The derivative does not exist because the slopes disagree.

pitfalls: 0/0 is an indeterminate form, not zero.
Continuity alone does not permit differentiation.

checks.explanation: Differentiability implies continuity. |x| is continuous at zero but its one-sided slopes disagree, so the reverse fails.

lessons.title: Derivatives, extrema and the mean value theorem
lessons.intuition: Derivatives reveal change, but a zero slope alone does not identify a maximum. The mean value theorem connects average change over an interval to an instantaneous slope inside it, under precise continuity and differentiability assumptions.

sections.title: Derivative rules
sections.body: Differentiate sums termwise; the product rule is (uv)′=u′v+uv′, not u′v′. The chain rule multiplies outer derivative by inner derivative. For a quotient use (u′v−uv′)/v² where v≠0. These rules follow from the difference quotient and simplify examining polynomial and composite functions.

sections.title: Finding extrema
sections.body: On a closed interval, a continuous function attains absolute extrema. List endpoints and interior critical points where derivative is zero or undefined; compare function values. A sign change from + to − in f′ gives a local maximum, from − to + a local minimum. If f′(c)=0, positive f″ gives a local minimum and negative f″ gives a maximum; f″=0 is inconclusive.

sections.title: Rolle and mean value theorems
sections.body: If f is continuous on [a,b], differentiable on (a,b), and f(a)=f(b), Rolle gives f′(c)=0 inside. The MVT removes the equal-endpoint requirement and gives f′(c)=[f(b)−f(a)]/(b−a). Verify assumptions before solving the slope equation; functions with corners can violate the conclusion.

sections.title: Classifying a stationary point by signs
sections.body: For f(x)=x³−3x, derivative is 3x²−3, vanishing at x=−1 and x=1. On x<−1 the derivative is positive, on −1<x<1 it is negative, and on x>1 it is positive. Thus −1 is a local maximum and 1 a local minimum. The second derivative 6x gives the same classification, but the sign test also handles cases where f″ is zero. To find absolute extrema over a given closed interval, compare only critical points inside that interval plus its endpoints. Rolle’s theorem is MVT with equal endpoint values: the average slope becomes zero. A nondifferentiable corner can invalidate the hypothesis even if endpoints match.

Do not omit endpoints for absolute extrema.

lessons.title: Integration and accumulated quantities
lessons.intuition: Integration sums contributions over a continuum. A definite integral is signed accumulation; area below the axis contributes negatively. An antiderivative reverses differentiation, but definite integrals become useful only after applying limits consistently.

sections.title: Fundamental theorem and basic rules
sections.body: If f is continuous, an antiderivative F satisfies ∫ₐᵇf(x)dx=F(b)−F(a). The indefinite integral includes an arbitrary constant C. For n≠−1, ∫xⁿdx=xⁿ⁺¹/(n+1)+C; ∫1/x dx=ln|x|+C on intervals avoiding zero. Definite integral limits have orientation: reversing them changes the sign.

sections.title: Substitution and parts
sections.body: For a composite expression, choose u=g(x) and du=g′(x)dx. In definite integrals, either transform both limits into u or substitute back before using original limits. Integration by parts is ∫u dv=uv−∫v du and is useful for products such as x eˣ or x ln x. Choose a differentiable part that simplifies.

sections.title: Symmetry and improper cases
sections.body: On [−a,a], an odd function integrates to zero and an even function integrates to twice the integral on [0,a]. This requires an integrable function; a singularity cannot be dismissed just by symmetry. For improper integrals use one-sided limits at singularities or infinity and require convergence.

sections.title: Integration by parts with actual evaluation
sections.body: To evaluate ∫₀¹xeˣdx, choose u=x and dv=eˣdx. Then du=dx and v=eˣ. Integration by parts gives [xeˣ]₀¹−∫₀¹eˣdx=e−(e−1)=1. lessons.title: Probability, conditional probability and Bayes
lessons.intuition: A conditional probability changes the population under consideration. Once B is known, count only outcomes inside B. Bayes reverses a conditioning direction by combining prior frequencies with evidence; a high detection rate need not imply a high probability that a detected condition is real.

sections.body: A probability measure assigns nonnegative values totaling 1 to the sample space. For P(B)>0, P(A|B)=P(A∩B)/P(B). The multiplication rule gives P(A∩B)=P(A|B)P(B). Mutually exclusive nonzero-probability events cannot be independent, because their intersection is empty.

sections.body: If B₁,…,Bₖ form a partition, P(A)=ΣP(A|Bᵢ)P(Bᵢ). Bayes gives P(Bⱼ|A)=P(A|Bⱼ)P(Bⱼ)/P(A). Construct the denominator from every way the evidence can occur. Use a frequency table when fractions feel abstract: population counts often make false positives obvious.

sections.body: Use rows for cause classes and columns for evidence outcomes. The formula agrees: 0.8×0.2/[0.8×0.2+0.1×0.8]. Independence can also be tested by checking whether conditioning leaves the probability unchanged. Sampling without replacement often destroys that equality because the first draw changes the remaining population.

steps: Imagine 10000 people: 100 have the condition, and 90 of them test positive.

steps: First draw is an ace with probability 4/52.
Given that, only 3 aces among 51 cards remain.
Multiply (4/52)(3/51)=1/221. Treating the draws as independent would use the wrong second factor.

pitfalls: P(A|B) is usually not P(B|A).
Disjointness and independence are different.

lessons.title: Random variables and descriptive statistics
lessons.intuition: A random variable attaches a number to an outcome. The distribution tells you how often values occur; expectation, variance, and quantiles summarize different aspects. An average alone cannot tell you whether values are tightly concentrated or widely spread.

sections.title: PMF, PDF and CDF
sections.body: For discrete X, p(x)=P(X=x) is a probability mass function and its values sum to 1. For continuous X, a density f integrates to 1; probabilities are areas, so P(X=x)=0 at individual points. The cumulative distribution F(x)=P(X≤x) works in both cases and is nondecreasing.

sections.title: Expectation and dispersion
sections.body: For discrete X, E[X]=Σxp(x); for continuous X, integrate xf(x). E[aX+b]=aE[X]+b without needing independence. Var(X)=E[X²]−E[X]² and Var(aX+b)=a²Var(X). Standard deviation is the square root of variance. Variances of sums add for independent variables; otherwise covariance terms matter.

sections.title: Mean, median and mode
sections.body: The arithmetic mean uses every observation and is sensitive to outliers. Median splits the ordered data into halves and resists extreme values. Mode is a most frequent value and need not be unique. Distinguish population variance, with divisor n, from the conventional unbiased sample variance, with divisor n−1, when the question specifies a sample estimator.

sections.title: Deriving variance and using linearity
sections.body: Variance is E[(X−μ)²], where μ=E[X]. Expand the square: E[X²−2μX+μ²]=E[X²]−2μE[X]+μ²=E[X²]−μ². This explains why the second moment, not just the mean, is needed. For a count X=I₁+…+Iₙ of indicator variables, E[X]=ΣE[Iᵢ]=ΣP(Iᵢ=1), even when the events are dependent. Variance addition requires checking covariance: Var(X+Y)=Var(X)+Var(Y)+2Cov(X,Y). Independent variables have covariance zero, but zero covariance alone does not establish independence in general. Scaling all observations by 3 scales deviations by 3 and squared deviations by 9, while adding a constant leaves deviations unchanged.

Sorted middle value is 2, so median=2; 2 also occurs most often, so mode=2.
The large observation shifts the mean away from the typical central values.

lessons.title: Binomial and Poisson distributions
lessons.intuition: The binomial distribution counts successes in a fixed number of independent identical trials. Poisson models event counts in a window with a specified mean rate. Identify the experiment first: fixed trials and success probability suggest binomial; an event rate over time suggests Poisson.

sections.title: Binomial construction
sections.body: X~Binomial(n,p) has P(X=k)=C(n,k)pᵏ(1−p)ⁿ⁻ᵏ. The combination chooses success positions; multiplying gives the probability of a specific ordering. E[X]=np and Var(X)=np(1−p). At least one success is conveniently 1−(1−p)ⁿ.

sections.title: Poisson counts
sections.body: X~Poisson(λ) has P(X=k)=e^(−λ)λᵏ/k!, k≥0. Its mean and variance are both λ. If the rate is r per unit time, a duration t has λ=rt under the homogeneous Poisson-process model. Independent Poisson counts add to a Poisson count with summed means.

sections.title: When approximation is sensible
sections.body: For many independent trials with small p and moderate np, Binomial(n,p) can be approximated by Poisson(np). It is an approximation, not a rule replacing all binomial questions. Check the event and units; changing a 1-minute window to 3 minutes multiplies λ by three, not p by three.

sections.title: Deriving binomial moments with indicators
sections.body: Write the success count X as the sum of n independent Bernoulli indicators Iᵢ. Each has mean p and variance p(1−p), so expectation is np and independent variances sum to np(1−p). The mass formula contains C(n,k) because there are that many ways to place k successes among n positions. For Poisson with rate 3/hour, a 20-minute interval has λ=1, not λ=3: converting the window is part of specifying the distribution. Then P(exactly two)=e⁻¹/2. A binomial n=1000,p=0.001 has mean 1; its zero-count probability (0.999)^1000 is close to e⁻¹, illustrating the rare-event approximation without treating it as an exact equality.

examples.prompt: Fair coin tossed four times: exactly two heads
steps: Choose the head positions in C(4,2)=6 ways.
Each ordering has probability (1/2)⁴=1/16, so the probability is 6/16=3/8.

examples.prompt: Calls arrive with rate 2 per minute. Find mean and zero-call probability in 3 minutes
steps: The window mean is λ=2×3=6.
Expected count is 6 and variance is 6.
P(X=0)=e⁻⁶6⁰/0!=e⁻⁶; the duration must be included before using the formula.

pitfalls: Binomial trials need the same p and independence.
Poisson λ belongs to the actual time window.

checks.explanation: Binomial counts successes under those three assumptions. A rate-based event count may instead use Poisson, and waiting time may be continuous.

lessons.title: Uniform, exponential and normal distributions
lessons.intuition: Continuous probabilities are interval areas. Uniform gives equal density over a bounded interval; exponential models waiting time with a constant hazard; normal describes symmetric variation around a mean. Each has a different support and interpretation.

sections.title: Uniform[a,b]
sections.body: The density is 1/(b−a) inside [a,b] and zero outside. An interval probability is its overlapping length divided by b−a. Mean=(a+b)/2 and variance=(b−a)²/12. Equal density does not mean a positive probability at each exact point; any one point still has probability zero.

sections.title: Exponential rate λ
sections.body: The density is λe^(−λx) for x≥0; survival P(X>t)=e^(−λt). Mean=1/λ and variance=1/λ². Memorylessness follows because P(X>s+t|X>s)=e^(−λ(s+t))/e^(−λs)=e^(−λt). The rate parameter is the reciprocal of the mean, so check which parameterization the question uses.

sections.title: Normal(μ,σ²)
sections.body: The density is symmetric around μ, so mean=median=mode=μ. Standardize using Z=(X−μ)/σ, not σ². Probabilities reduce to standard normal CDF Φ: P(a<X<b)=Φ((b−μ)/σ)−Φ((a−μ)/σ). Independent normal variables have normal sums with means and variances added.

sections.title: Normalize a density before calculating probabilities
sections.body: If f(x)=cx on [0,2] and zero outside, normalization requires ∫₀²cx dx=2c=1, so c=1/2. Then P(1<X<2)=∫₁²x/2 dx=3/4, and E[X]=∫₀²x²/2 dx=4/3. description: From Boolean expressions to working circuits

lessons.title: Boolean algebra and algebraic minimization
lessons.intuition: Boolean simplification preserves a function while reducing the gates required to implement it. Work with identities valid for every input. Boolean addition is OR, so 1+1=1; ordinary numerical cancellation cannot be imported without checking it.

sections.title: Basic identities
sections.body: Identity laws give A+0=A and A·1=A; domination gives A+1=1 and A·0=0. Complement gives A+¬A=1 and A¬A=0. Idempotence gives A+A=A and AA=A. Absorption A+AB=A removes a redundant condition. De Morgan moves negation through a gate and swaps AND with OR.

sections.title: Canonical forms
sections.body: A minterm specifies every variable and is true on exactly one truth-table row. Sum the minterms where the function is 1 to obtain canonical SOP. A maxterm is false on exactly one row; multiply maxterms for rows where the function is 0 to obtain canonical POS. Ordinary simplified SOP need not contain every variable in every term.

sections.title: Simplifying systematically
sections.body: Combine terms differing in only one literal: AB+A¬B=A(B+¬B)=A. Remove absorbed terms and apply the consensus rule XY+¬XZ+YZ=XY+¬XZ. Confirm the result with a truth table when unsure. Fewer literals and fewer gates are related but distinct implementation cost measures.

steps: Factor the first two terms: A(B+¬B)=A.
Now F=A+AC.
Absorption removes AC, leaving F=A for all inputs.

examples.prompt: Build SOP for a 2-variable function true on 01 and 11
steps: The corresponding minterms are ¬AB and AB.
F=¬AB+AB=B(¬A+A).
The simplified expression is B, so the output ignores A.

pitfalls: Boolean OR is not arithmetic addition.
A canonical term must contain every variable.

checks.prompt: Which algebraic law explains A+AB=A?
checks.hint: The second term is already contained in the first condition.
checks.explanation: Absorption removes AB because whenever AB is true, A is already true; it adds no new accepting assignments.

checks.hint: B and C remain unconstrained.
checks.explanation: Fix A=1; B and C each have 2 choices, yielding 4.

lessons.title: Karnaugh maps and the tabular method
lessons.intuition: Adjacent minterms differ in one variable, so combining them eliminates that variable. Karnaugh maps make this adjacency visual; the tabular method performs the same operation symbolically and scales without relying on a drawing.

sections.title: K-map layout and grouping
sections.body: Use Gray-code labels such as 00,01,11,10 so neighbours differ in one bit. Group 1s in rectangles with 1,2,4,8,… cells. Edges wrap around and corners may be adjacent; diagonal cells are not adjacent. A group with 2ᵏ cells eliminates k variables. Overlap is allowed and often necessary; every required 1 must be covered.

sections.title: Prime and essential implicants
sections.body: A prime implicant cannot be enlarged into another valid group. An essential prime implicant covers a minterm covered by no other prime implicant and must be selected. After selecting essentials, cover remaining minterms with a low-cost collection. Don’t-care cells may be included as 1s to enlarge a group or ignored; there is no requirement to cover them.

sections.title: Quine–McCluskey
sections.body: Write minterms in binary, group by number of 1s, and combine terms differing in one specified bit, replacing that bit by a dash. Repeat until no more combinations are possible. Uncombined terms are prime implicants. Build a chart mapping primes to covered required minterms and select a cover. This separates implicant generation from the covering problem.

steps: The minterms are 000,001,010,011.
Across the four-cell group B and C take both values but A stays 0.
Eliminate B,C to get F=¬A.
They differ only in the final bit.
Replace that position by a dash: 101−.
For variables A,B,C,D the product is A¬BC; D is eliminated.

pitfalls: K-map labels use Gray order, not binary numeric order.
Larger groups should not include required zero cells.

lessons.title: Designing combinational circuits
lessons.intuition: A combinational circuit has no memory: outputs are determined by current inputs. The design process starts with a behavioural specification, translates it to a truth table, simplifies the output equations, and maps them to available gates or modules.

sections.title: Adders and arithmetic building blocks
sections.body: A half adder produces sum A⊕B and carry AB. A full adder includes Cin: sum=A⊕B⊕Cin and Cout=AB+ACin+BCin. Cascading full adders yields a ripple-carry adder whose worst delay grows with the carry path length. A carry-lookahead adder uses generate G=AB and propagate P=A⊕B to compute carry dependencies more directly.

sections.title: Multiplexers and decoders
sections.body: A 2ᵏ:1 multiplexer selects one of 2ᵏ data inputs using k select bits. A decoder maps k inputs to up to 2ᵏ one-hot outputs. Implement a Boolean function with a mux by assigning select variables, then making each data input the residual function of remaining variables. Decoder minterm outputs can be ORed for SOP implementation.

sections.title: Design and timing
sections.body: Validate all input combinations, including active-high/active-low control conventions. Gates have propagation delays; the longest input-to-output path determines worst-case settling. lessons.title: Sequential circuits, flip-flops and state machines
lessons.intuition: Sequential circuits combine current inputs with stored state. To reason correctly, distinguish what is stored now, what will be stored at the next clock event, and which outputs depend on inputs immediately.

sections.title: Storage elements
sections.body: A level-sensitive latch can change while its enable is active; an edge-triggered flip-flop samples around a clock edge. For D flip-flops Qnext=D; for T flip-flops Qnext=Q⊕T. JK devices hold for 00, reset for 01, set for 10 and toggle for 11. Setup and hold intervals constrain how stable inputs must be around the sampling edge.

sections.title: State-machine construction
sections.body: List states and draw input-labelled transitions. A Moore output depends only on state; a Mealy output depends on state and current input. Assign binary state codes, derive next-state/output truth tables, simplify logic and select storage. k flip-flops can encode at most 2ᵏ states, so n states require ceiling(log₂n) bits.

sections.title: Counters and timing
sections.body: A synchronous counter clocks all flip-flops together; ripple counters cascade transitions and have accumulated delays. A modulo-n counter uses n reachable states and returns to its start. Include reset behaviour and handle unused state codes so a stray state does not trap the machine. Clock period must allow launch, combinational delay and destination setup margin.

steps: Need 10 distinct states.

lessons.title: Fixed point, floating point and overflow
lessons.prerequisite: Binary notation and powers of two.
lessons.intuition: Bits do not have an inherent numeric interpretation. The same pattern may represent unsigned data, a signed integer, or a fraction depending on the agreed encoding. Arithmetic questions must specify width, sign convention and scaling before calculation.

sections.title: Integer representations
sections.body: Unsigned n-bit values span 0 to 2ⁿ−1. Two’s complement spans −2ⁿ⁻¹ to 2ⁿ⁻¹−1; its most significant bit has weight −2ⁿ⁻¹. Negate within a fixed width by complementing all bits and adding 1. Sign extension repeats the sign bit to preserve a two’s-complement value. Carry-out concerns unsigned overflow; signed addition overflows when equal-sign operands produce an opposite-sign result.

sections.title: Fixed-point scaling
sections.body: With f fractional bits, interpret the stored integer as I/2ᶠ. An unsigned n-bit fixed-point format has step size 2⁻ᶠ and maximum (2ⁿ−1)/2ᶠ. Signed formats use a signed stored integer with the same scaling. Addition requires aligned scaling; multiplying two scaled integers doubles the fractional-bit count until rescaled.

sections.title: IEEE 754 single precision
sections.body: There are 1 sign bit, 8 exponent bits and 23 stored fraction bits. Normal numbers have value (−1)ˢ(1.f)2^(E−127). E=0 reserves zero and subnormal values; E=255 reserves infinities and NaNs. The implicit leading 1 applies only to normals. Rounding means real-number associativity need not hold numerically.

pitfalls: Two’s-complement range is asymmetric.

Carry and signed overflow are different.

name: Computer Organization & Architecture
description: Understand what happens beneath your code

lessons.title: Instruction sets, addressing modes and CPU time
lessons.intuition: An instruction is a compact command that tells a processor what operation to perform and where operands come from. Addressing modes separate operand-location rules from the operation itself. CPU performance follows the total work and cycles, not clock rate alone.

sections.title: Instruction structure
sections.body: An instruction can contain an opcode, register identifiers, addressing-mode bits and immediate/displacement fields. Load/store architectures generally operate on registers and use separate memory-transfer instructions; other architectures may permit memory operands directly. The program counter identifies instruction flow, and branches update it differently from ordinary sequential execution.

sections.title: Effective addresses
sections.body: Immediate addressing embeds the operand, not an address. Register addressing reads the register value. Direct addressing uses an explicit address; indirect addressing follows a pointer to the operand. Base+displacement computes EA=base+offset; indexed modes add an index, sometimes scaled by element size. PC-relative addressing uses a displacement from a specified PC reference point; conventions matter.

sections.title: Performance equation
sections.body: CPU time=instruction count×average CPI×cycle time=IC×CPI/frequency. For instruction classes, average CPI=Σfractionᵢ×CPIᵢ. A new design may use fewer instructions but more cycles each. Compare complete execution time and use speedup=old time/new time.

examples.prompt: Address an array element using base 1000, index 3 and 4-byte elements
steps: The byte displacement is 3×4=12.
Using raw index 3 as a byte offset would fetch the wrong location.

examples.prompt: Compute time for 2 million instructions, CPI 3, clock 1 GHz
steps: Total cycles=2×10⁶×3=6×10⁶.
Cycle time is 1/10⁹ seconds.
CPU time=0.006 s=6 ms.

pitfalls: Bytes, words and elements are different address units.
Average CPI must weight instruction frequencies.

lessons.title: ALU design and hardwired/microprogrammed control
lessons.intuition: The datapath performs operations; the control unit chooses which operation happens and when. Keeping those roles separate makes it possible to trace an instruction as a sequence of register transfers instead of treating the CPU as a black box.

sections.title: ALU and status flags
sections.body: An ALU combines an adder, logic functions and selection hardware. Subtraction can reuse addition by complementing the second operand and setting carry-in: A−B=A+¬B+1. Flags may record zero, sign, carry and signed overflow. Signed comparison cannot rely on the sign of a wrapped subtraction without considering overflow.

sections.title: Register-transfer sequencing
sections.body: An instruction fetch can involve MAR←PC, memory read, IR←memory data and PC advancement. Execution then reads operands, activates the ALU, and writes a destination. Control signals choose mux inputs, register write enables, ALU function and memory actions. A single-cycle design combines actions in one long cycle; multicycle designs reuse hardware across shorter steps.

sections.title: Control implementation
sections.body: Hardwired control uses finite-state logic and decoding to generate signals, often with low latency but less flexibility. Microprogrammed control stores control words in a control memory; a sequencer chooses subsequent microinstructions using opcode and conditions. Horizontal microcode exposes more parallel control bits, while encoded vertical microcode reduces width at the cost of decoding.

lessons.title: Memory hierarchy and cache mapping
lessons.prerequisite: Binary address splitting and CPU performance.
lessons.intuition: Caches exploit repetition and neighbourhood in memory accesses. A small fast store holds copies of slower memory blocks. Mapping decides where a block may go; replacement decides which resident block leaves when those allowed locations are full.

sections.title: Hierarchy and locality
sections.body: Temporal locality reuses recently accessed data; spatial locality accesses nearby addresses. Transfers occur in blocks, so one miss may bring several adjacent words. A larger block can improve spatial reuse but reduces the number of resident blocks at fixed capacity and increases transfer cost. Separate compulsory, capacity and conflict misses when reasoning about changes.

sections.title: Address partition
sections.body: In a byte-addressed system with 2ᵇ-byte blocks, the lowest b bits are block offset. A cache with S sets needs log₂S index bits; remaining high bits form the tag. Direct mapping has one line per set; W-way associativity has W lines per set. Sets=capacity/(block size×ways). Fully associative caches have one set and no index bits.

sections.title: Writes and performance
sections.body: Write-through updates lower memory on writes; write-back marks lines dirty and writes them on eviction. Write-allocate versus no-write-allocate controls write misses independently. Single-level AMAT=hit time+miss rate×miss penalty, where the penalty is the additional miss cost. Multilevel formulas require using local versus global miss rates consistently.

examples.prompt: Split a 32-bit address for a 16 KiB, 4-way cache with 64-byte blocks
steps: Offset bits=log₂64=6; index bits=log₂64=6.
Tag bits=32−6−6=20. Capacity alone does not determine index bits without associativity.

examples.prompt: Compute AMAT for hit time 2 ns, miss rate 4%, penalty 50 ns
steps: Miss contribution is 0.04×50=2 ns.
Add the baseline hit time 2 ns.
AMAT=4 ns; do not multiply the hit time by hit rate in this penalty-based convention.

pitfalls: Cache capacity usually excludes tag/valid/dirty storage unless specified.
Use number of sets, not total lines, for index bits.

checks.hint: A set-associative cache indexes a set, then compares tags within it.
checks.explanation: Index width is log₂(number of sets). Number of sets equals lines divided by ways; total lines works only in direct mapping.

checks.hint: Use the penalty convention.

lessons.title: Memory interfacing, interrupts and DMA
lessons.intuition: A processor must select the correct memory device and coordinate data transfer. I/O introduces devices whose speed and readiness differ from the CPU. Polling, interrupts and DMA assign different amounts of coordination work to software and hardware.

sections.title: Memory organization and decoding
sections.body: A memory specified as N×w stores N locations of w bits each. Address bits select locations; data pins carry width w. To expand width, connect chips to different data-bit lanes while sharing address lines. To expand depth, decode extra high address bits into chip-select signals. Byte addressing may require multiple byte lanes and enables.

sections.title: Polling and interrupts
sections.body: Polling repeatedly checks a device status register and spends CPU cycles waiting. An interrupt lets a device request attention; the CPU saves required execution state, enters an interrupt handler, services the event and returns. Masking, priority and nesting determine which interrupts can be serviced. Interrupt latency includes finishing or suspending permitted work and reaching the handler.

sections.title: DMA
sections.body: A DMA controller transfers blocks between a device and memory after the CPU configures addresses, length and direction. Burst mode may occupy a bus for a sequence; cycle stealing interleaves transfers with CPU activity. DMA reduces per-byte CPU overhead but does not imply zero setup cost or unlimited bandwidth. Shared caches can require coherency handling for DMA buffers.

steps: Width expansion requires 16/8=2 chips in parallel per bank.
Depth expansion requires 4K/1K=4 banks.
Total=2×4=8 chips; two extra address bits select the bank, while ten bits select a location inside a chip.

examples.prompt: Compare one-byte interrupts with DMA for 4096 bytes
steps: An interrupt per byte produces 4096 service events.
A DMA block can use one setup and a completion interrupt under the simple model.
The CPU saves many handler invocations, although memory-bus transfer time remains.

pitfalls: Chip width and depth expansion are separate factors.
DMA still competes for memory bandwidth.
revision: Total chips=(desired depth/chip depth)×(desired width/chip width).
Interrupts request service; DMA performs data movement.

lessons.title: Instruction pipelining and hazards
lessons.intuition: Pipelining overlaps different instructions in different stages. It increases completed instructions per unit time, while each individual instruction still passes through every stage. Hazards arise when that ideal overlap would violate resource limits or program dependencies.

sections.title: Ideal timing
sections.body: For k equal-latency stages and n instructions, an initially empty ideal pipeline takes k+n−1 cycles. The first instruction fills the pipeline; each subsequent one then finishes one cycle later. Clock period is determined by the slowest stage plus pipeline-register overhead, not average stage delay. Unequal stages reduce ideal speedup.

sections.title: Data and structural hazards
sections.body: A structural hazard occurs when simultaneous operations need the same unavailable resource. A RAW dependency requires a consumer to receive the producer’s value; forwarding can route it before register writeback. A load-use pair can still stall if data arrives after the consumer needs it. WAR and WAW are naming/order hazards relevant to designs that reorder reads or writes; simple in-order pipelines handle them differently.

sections.title: Control hazards
sections.body: A branch may make fetched instructions wrong-path work. Waiting, predicting, or delayed-branch mechanisms handle this in different models. A misprediction flushes invalid instructions and adds cycles. To compute effective CPI, add expected stall cycles per instruction from hazards without double-counting overlapping penalties.

examples.prompt: A 5-stage pipeline runs 12 instructions with 3 total stall cycles
steps: Ideal cycles=5+12−1=16.
Add the specified actual stalls: 16+3=19.
At 2 ns per cycle total elapsed time is 38 ns, not 12×5×2.

examples.prompt: A branch frequency is 20%, misprediction rate 10%, penalty 3 cycles
steps: Mispredictions per instruction=0.2×0.1=0.02.
Expected additional CPI=0.02×3=0.06.
If baseline CPI is 1 and there are no other stalls, effective CPI=1.06.

pitfalls: Dependency does not automatically mean a stall if forwarding meets timing.
Pipeline speedup is not simply stage count for short sequences.
revision: Clock period follows the slowest stage.

checks.explanation: Forwarding can resolve many RAW dependencies without a stall. A load-use timing gap may still require one in the specified pipeline.

name: Programming & Data Structures
description: Build a strong foundation in C and structures

lessons.title: C types, expressions, pointers and memory
lessons.intuition: C exposes the relationship between a value and its storage. A pointer stores an address; dereferencing accesses the object there. Tracing code requires tracking types, lifetimes and sequencing, rather than assuming every expression has a predictable machine result.

sections.title: Types and evaluation
sections.body: Integer promotions and conversions affect arithmetic. Integer division truncates toward zero; floating operands change division behaviour. Logical AND and logical OR short-circuit, evaluating the right side only when necessary. sizeof measures bytes and normally does not evaluate its operand, except relevant variable-length-array cases. Do not assume int is always four bytes unless the question states the machine model.

sections.title: Pointers and arrays
sections.body: For a pointer p to T, p+1 advances by sizeof(T) bytes within a valid array range. An array expression usually decays to a pointer to its first element, but sizeof on an actual in-scope array returns full array size. Function parameters written as arrays are adjusted to pointers. Dereferencing a one-past-the-end pointer is invalid even though forming it is permitted.

sections.title: Lifetime and undefined behaviour
sections.body: Automatic local objects cease to exist after their scope exits; returning their addresses creates dangling pointers. Dynamically allocated storage survives until freed and must be checked for allocation failure. Out-of-bounds accesses and unsequenced conflicting modifications can be undefined behaviour. For such programs, reporting a single numerical output is not a valid analysis.

sections.title: A safe pointer trace
sections.body: Use a table of variable, type, value and referenced object. In the example, a is an array object, p points to its second element, and *p refers to a[1]. After *p=9, the array changes without changing p. Moving p by one advances to a[2]; it does not increase the integer stored at a[1]. A pointer may be formed one past the array, but that location is not an element to dereference. The code deliberately separates updates into sequenced statements to avoid unsequenced modification traps.

steps: For int a[5], sizeof(a)=5×4=20 bytes while a remains an array in scope.
If p=&a[1], p+2 points to a[3], advancing 8 bytes.
Inside a function f(int a[]), sizeof(a) is pointer size, not 20.
7 and 2 are integer operands, so 7/2 gives 3.
2.0 is floating; 7 is converted and division gives 3.5.
Assigning the first expression to double afterward produces 3.0; conversion does not restore the discarded fraction.

lessons.title: Recursion and stack-frame tracing
lessons.intuition: A recursive call is another invocation with its own local state. You can reason inductively about the returned value or mechanically trace stack frames. Both require knowing where recursion stops and how an argument gets closer to that base case.

sections.title: Call and return model
sections.body: Each call creates a frame with parameters, locals and return information. A recursive call suspends its caller until it returns. For factorial, fact(n) waits for fact(n−1), then multiplies. Statements before recursion run on descent; statements after recursion run during unwinding. Shared global state differs from per-frame locals.

sections.title: Correctness and termination
sections.body: State a base case and a decreasing measure bounded below, such as remaining input length. An induction proof assumes smaller calls work and verifies the current combination. Recursion over graph edges needs a visited set when cycles are possible; merely calling neighbours is not guaranteed to terminate.

sections.title: Time versus space
sections.body: Count the total calls for time and maximum simultaneous active frames for stack space. Factorial takes Θ(n) time and Θ(n) stack. A balanced divide recursion can take Θ(n) total work but Θ(log n) stack depth. Naive Fibonacci revisits subproblems exponentially; memoization stores repeated results and reduces time to Θ(n).

lessons.title: Arrays, linked lists, stacks and queues
lessons.intuition: Data structures trade access speed against update cost. A complexity statement must specify what information you already possess: inserting after a known linked-list node is cheap, but finding that node may dominate the operation.

sections.title: Arrays and linked lists
sections.body: Contiguous arrays allow constant-time indexed access because address=base+index×element size. Middle insertion shifts a suffix, taking Θ(n). A singly linked list stores a next pointer and supports O(1) insertion after a known node. Finding a predecessor or an indexed element takes O(n). Doubly linked lists store previous links too, enabling deletion of a known node without a predecessor search.

sections.title: Stacks and queues
sections.body: Stacks remove the most recently inserted item and support recursion, expression evaluation and DFS. Queues remove the oldest and support BFS. A linked queue can enqueue at the tail and dequeue at the head in O(1) with both pointers. Reversing these ends in a singly linked list makes tail deletion expensive.

sections.title: Circular arrays
sections.body: Advance queue indices modulo capacity. Empty and full can both appear as head=tail unless you track a count, a full flag, or leave one slot unused. A capacity-n array with an unused-slot convention holds only n−1 elements. Carefully check whether an index denotes the next free location or the last occupied location.

sections.title: Linked queue operation sequence
sections.body: To enqueue a node, initialize its next pointer to NULL, attach it after the current tail if one exists, or make it the head for an empty queue; then update tail. To dequeue, read the head node, advance head to its next, and if the queue becomes empty set tail to NULL as well. Save the returned value before freeing the removed node. These pointer operations are O(1) because no predecessor search is required. A nonempty invariant is that tail points to the final node and tail.next is NULL. The empty invariant has both pointers NULL. Missing the final tail reset leaves a dangling pointer after removing the last node.

lessons.title: Trees, traversals and binary search trees
lessons.intuition: A tree is a connected acyclic structure. Rooting it introduces parents, children and subtrees. Binary search trees add an ordering invariant, so searching can discard one entire subtree at each comparison—but only balanced height guarantees logarithmic depth.

sections.title: Tree terminology and traversals
sections.body: Height in edges is the longest root-to-leaf edge count; some problems instead count nodes, so read the convention. Preorder visits root,left,right; inorder left,root,right; postorder left,right,root. A binary tree has at most two children per node. A full binary tree gives each internal node exactly two children; a complete tree fills levels left to right.

sections.title: BST operations
sections.body: For distinct keys, everything in a node’s left subtree is smaller and everything in the right is larger. Search follows one comparison-directed path. Insertion finds a null child location. Deletion handles no child, one child, or two children; the two-child case replaces the key with inorder successor or predecessor and deletes that replacement node.

sections.title: Complexity and reconstruction
sections.body: Search, insertion and deletion take O(h). Sorted insertion into an unbalanced BST can create h=n−1. Balanced trees maintain logarithmic height. Inorder traversal produces sorted keys, not insertion order. With distinct keys, inorder plus preorder or postorder uniquely determine a binary tree; preorder alone generally does not determine an arbitrary binary tree.

sections.title: Why traversal order changes output
sections.body: The recursive structure is the same for all three depth-first traversals; only the placement of visit(root) changes. Put it before the two recursive calls for preorder, between them for inorder, or afterward for postorder. On a BST, the between placement visits every smaller left key, then the root, then every larger right key, proving sorted output by induction. All three traversals visit each node once and take Θ(n) time; auxiliary recursive space is Θ(h), which is Θ(n) for a chain and Θ(log n) for a balanced tree.

    inorder(node.left)
    visit(node.key)
    inorder(node.right)

lessons.title: Binary heaps and graph representations
lessons.intuition: A heap guarantees an extreme value at the root without sorting the entire collection. Graph representations instead organize many-to-many links. In both cases, choosing a representation determines which operations are cheap and which information must be searched.

sections.title: Heap invariants
sections.body: A binary min-heap is a complete binary tree whose parent key is no larger than its child keys. In a zero-based array, left child=2i+1, right child=2i+2 and parent=floor((i−1)/2). Completeness gives height Θ(log n). Sibling order is unrestricted and a heap is not a BST.

sections.title: Heap updates and construction
sections.body: Insertion appends and bubbles upward; delete-min swaps the final element to the root and sifts downward. Each traverses at most the height. Bottom-up construction sifts internal nodes from the last parent backward. It is Θ(n), since many nodes have tiny subtrees; multiplying n by the maximum sift cost overestimates aggregate work.

sections.title: Graph storage
sections.body: An adjacency matrix uses Θ(V²) space and permits O(1) edge tests, but listing neighbours takes Θ(V). Adjacency lists use Θ(V+E) space and enumerate neighbours proportional to degree. An undirected graph usually stores each edge twice in lists. Weighted graphs attach weights; directed graphs distinguish outgoing from incoming edges.

sections.title: Why build-heap is linear
sections.body: Only about n/2 nodes have height zero, at most n/4 have height one, at most n/8 have height two, and so on. A sift from height h costs O(h), so aggregate work is bounded by n times Σh/2^(h+1), a convergent constant sum. Thus bottom-up build is O(n), unlike repeatedly inserting n elements, whose simple worst-case bound is O(n log n). The algorithm starts at the last internal node, floor(n/2)−1 in zero-based indexing, and visits parents backward. Each node’s child subtrees are already heaps before it is sifted, which is the key invariant.

A full adjacency matrix allocates 1000000 cells.
Adjacency-list edge entries are 2000 directed or 4000 undirected, plus vertex headers.
Sparse connectivity strongly favours list space, though a matrix provides constant-time edge membership tests.

Array child formulas change for one-based indexing.
revision: Heap insert/delete Θ(log n), bottom-up build Θ(n).
List space Θ(V+E), matrix space Θ(V²).

name: Algorithms
description: Learn to choose, prove and analyze algorithms

lessons.title: Asymptotic time, space and recurrences
lessons.intuition: Asymptotic analysis studies how cost grows with input size. It abstracts constants but must still describe the operation being measured and the case: worst-case, average-case or amortized. A bound without those assumptions can mislead.

sections.title: Bounds and cases
sections.body: f=O(g) means f is eventually at most a constant multiple of g; Ω is a lower bound and Θ is both. A worst-case time function maximizes over size-n inputs. Average-case needs an input distribution; amortized cost averages over an operation sequence without necessarily involving randomness. Best-case O(n) does not imply worst-case O(n).

sections.title: Loops and recursion
sections.body: Consecutive loops add costs; nested loops sum inner counts. A triangular loop executes Σᵢ₌₁ⁿi=n(n+1)/2 operations. Halving a variable repeatedly yields Θ(log n) iterations. For T(n)=aT(n/b)+f(n), compare f with n^(log_b a) under the Master theorem’s applicable conditions; irregular recurrences may need a recursion tree or substitution.

sections.title: Space accounting
sections.body: Report input storage and auxiliary storage separately. Recursive stack memory follows the maximum active depth and frame size. Sequential calls reuse stack space once previous calls return. An algorithm can run Θ(n log n) total time with only Θ(log n) recursive stack if frames use constant additional space and divide inputs without copying.

sections.title: A recursion-tree comparison
sections.body: T(n)=T(n/2)+1 does constant work at each of log₂n levels, giving Θ(log n). T(n)=2T(n/2)+1 has increasingly many nodes and Θ(n) total calls. T(n)=2T(n/2)+n has total n work at each of logarithmically many levels, giving Θ(n log n). All three have logarithmic depth, demonstrating why depth is not a time bound. For an iterative doubling loop i=1;i<n;i*=2, iterations also grow logarithmically; a triangular incrementing loop instead requires summing linearly increasing counts. Specify input size in units that match the algorithm: numeric value n and bit length log n are not the same complexity parameter.

lessons.title: Searching and sorting with invariants
lessons.intuition: A search or sort is easier to understand through its invariant: what remains true after every iteration or recursive step. Complexity then follows from how fast the unresolved region shrinks and how much work is done to combine results.

sections.title: Binary search
sections.body: Maintain a range that could contain the key in sorted data. Compare its midpoint, discard the half ruled out by ordering, and update bounds so the loop progresses. After k comparisons the candidate range is about n/2ᵏ, producing Θ(log n) worst-case time. Unsorted input destroys the discard argument. Boundary variants such as first occurrence need their own invariant.

sections.title: Comparison sorts
sections.body: Insertion sort maintains a sorted prefix and inserts each new key, giving Θ(n²) worst-case and Θ(n) best-case on already sorted input. Merge sort recursively sorts halves and linearly merges them, giving Θ(n log n) and ordinarily Θ(n) auxiliary array storage. Heapsort builds a heap then repeatedly extracts, giving Θ(n log n) worst-case and an in-place array implementation.

sections.title: Quicksort and lower bounds
sections.body: Partition around a pivot, then recurse on both sides. Balanced partitions produce Θ(n log n); consistently extreme pivots produce Θ(n²). Randomization gives expected Θ(n log n), not a worst-case guarantee. General comparison sorting needs Ω(n log n) comparisons in the worst case; counting/radix sorts exploit additional assumptions and are not counterexamples.

sections.title: Binary search with terminating bounds
sections.body: This version keeps an inclusive range [lo,hi]. On a failed comparison it removes the midpoint as well as the impossible half, ensuring progress even when one or two candidates remain. The midpoint formula avoids unnecessarily adding two large indices in fixed-width arithmetic. The returned −1 distinguishes absence from valid zero-based index 0. Sorting the input is a prerequisite; this routine does not verify that condition.
sections.code:
binary_search(a, key):
    lo = 0; hi = length(a) - 1
    while lo <= hi:
        mid = lo + floor((hi-lo)/2)
        if a[mid] == key: return mid
        if a[mid] < key: lo = mid + 1
        else: hi = mid - 1
    return -1
