Return index 3. The invariant held because the array was sorted.
Compare front elements and take 1, then 2, then 3.
Take 4, then 8; one input is exhausted.
Append remaining 9. Each element is moved once, so merging six elements is linear.

pitfalls: Quicksort expected performance is not its worst case.
Binary search requires the monotonic ordering condition.
revision: Merge/heap worst-case Θ(n log n); quicksort worst-case Θ(n²).
Comparison sorting lower bound Ω(n log n).

lessons.title: Hashing, collisions and probing
lessons.intuition: A hash function chooses a bucket from a key. Different keys may choose the same bucket, so collision resolution is part of the data structure, not an exceptional error. Expected constant-time behaviour depends on hashing quality and load, not just using the word “hash”.

sections.title: Separate chaining
sections.body: Each bucket holds a collection of colliding entries. With m buckets and n keys, load factor α=n/m is the average chain length. Under a uniform hashing assumption, searches take expected O(1+α). Chaining permits α>1, while long or adversarially concentrated chains can still produce O(n) worst-case search.

sections.title: Open addressing
sections.body: All entries occupy slots in the array. Linear probing tries h(k),h(k)+1,… modulo m, causing primary clustering. Quadratic probing and double hashing use different probe sequences with coverage conditions. The table must have empty space for ordinary insertion; load factor approaches 1 with worsening probe costs.

sections.title: Deletion and invariants
sections.body: An unsuccessful search can stop at a never-used empty slot. Deleting by making a slot simply empty can break a probe chain and hide later entries. Use a tombstone or a correct relocation strategy. Resizing rehashes existing keys because the mapping depends on the new capacity; copying old slot positions is not sufficient.

sections.title: A probing trace with wraparound
sections.body: With capacity 7 and h(k)=k mod 7, insert 6,13,20,27 by linear probing. All initially choose slot 6. The first occupies 6; the second wraps to 0; the third checks 6,0 and occupies 1; the fourth occupies 2. This creates a cluster spanning the boundary. Searching for absent key 34 probes those occupied slots before reaching empty slot 3. The cost depends on occupied runs, not simply whether its initial hash is in range. A tombstone should not stop unsuccessful search, but insertion may remember its position for reuse while continuing sufficiently far to rule out an existing duplicate key.

lessons.title: Greedy and divide-and-conquer design
lessons.intuition: Divide-and-conquer solves smaller problems and combines their answers. Greedy algorithms instead commit to a local choice without revisiting it. A plausible local rule is not enough: prove why an optimal solution can include that choice.

sections.title: Divide-and-conquer pattern
sections.body: Define a base case, split into smaller subproblems, recursively solve, and combine. Merge sort uses two independent halves; binary search recurses into only one. Write a recurrence including the combine cost. Balanced splitting gives shallow recursion; an unbalanced split may erase the expected benefit.

sections.title: Greedy correctness
sections.body: State the local choice and residual problem. An exchange argument takes an optimal solution and replaces part of it with the greedy choice without worsening its objective, then applies induction. In activity selection, choosing the earliest-finishing compatible activity leaves the largest opportunity for subsequent activities.

sections.title: Where greedy fails
sections.body: Fractional knapsack sorts by value/weight ratio because fractional exchange is allowed. 0/1 knapsack forbids splitting, so the same strategy can miss a better combination. A counterexample is sufficient to disprove an unsupported greedy rule. MST algorithms work because cut/cycle properties justify their choices, not because every weighted optimization is greedy-solvable.

lessons.title: Dynamic programming from state to solution
lessons.intuition: Dynamic programming remembers answers to overlapping subproblems. Its difficult part is choosing what information a state must retain. Begin with a precise meaning for each table entry; a recurrence is valid only if it considers every allowed final choice.

sections.title: State and transition
sections.body: Define state variables, then express an answer using smaller states. For 0/1 knapsack dp[i,w] is maximum value using the first i items within capacity w. Skipping item i gives dp[i−1,w]; including it, when feasible, gives valueᵢ+dp[i−1,w−weightᵢ]. The maximum covers both possibilities.

sections.title: Base cases and ordering
sections.body: For knapsack, dp[0,w]=0 and dp[i,0]=0 when item weights are positive. Bottom-up order must make dependencies available; memoized recursion computes states on demand. A one-dimensional 0/1 knapsack update processes capacities downward so an item is not used multiple times in the same iteration. Upward updates correspond to a different reuse model.

sections.title: Cost and reconstruction
sections.body: Complexity is number of reachable states times transition cost, not simply recursion depth. O(nW) knapsack depends on numeric capacity W and is pseudopolynomial in its binary encoding length. To recover selected items, record choices or compare table entries and walk backwards. Finding only the optimal value need not reveal a unique solution.

sections.title: 0/1 knapsack in one dimension
sections.body: Process capacities downward so dp[w−weight] still refers to the state before the current item was introduced. An upward loop could read a value updated earlier during the same item and count that item again. For a single item weight 2,value 3 and capacity 4, downward iteration gives dp[4]=3 and dp[2]=3; upward iteration can incorrectly produce dp[4]=6 for a 0/1 problem.

Wrong iteration direction can silently turn 0/1 knapsack into unbounded reuse.

lessons.title: Graph traversal, MSTs and shortest paths
lessons.prerequisite: Graph representations, heaps and greedy proofs.
lessons.intuition: Graph traversal answers reachability; shortest paths minimize route cost; a minimum spanning tree minimizes the total cost of connecting every vertex. These objectives differ, so an MST path need not be a shortest path.

sections.title: BFS and DFS
sections.body: BFS uses a queue and discovers vertices in layers, giving shortest edge-count paths in an unweighted graph. DFS uses recursion or a stack, finishing one branch before another. DFS supports cycle detection and topological order for directed acyclic graphs. Using adjacency lists, both inspect vertices and edges in O(V+E); mark vertices when enqueued to avoid duplicate expansion.

sections.title: MST algorithms
sections.body: For a connected undirected weighted graph, a spanning tree has V−1 edges. Kruskal sorts edges by weight and uses disjoint sets to reject cycles. Prim grows one tree by repeatedly adding a cheapest edge leaving its current vertex set. The cut property justifies these choices. Disconnected input produces a minimum spanning forest rather than one spanning tree.

sections.title: Weighted shortest paths
sections.body: Dijkstra finalizes the smallest tentative distance and requires nonnegative weights for that greedy argument. Bellman–Ford relaxes every edge repeatedly and detects a reachable negative cycle via further improvement after V−1 rounds. Floyd–Warshall permits intermediate vertices one by one and runs O(V³) for all pairs. Relaxation tests whether dist[u]+w(u,v) improves dist[v].

An MST minimizes total tree weight, not each path.

lessons.title: BFS, DFS, cycles and topological ordering
lessons.intuition: A traversal marks each vertex once but chooses a different order for the frontier. BFS explores by distance in edges; DFS explores one path and then backtracks. That order determines what additional information you can safely infer.

sections.title: BFS levels
sections.body: Start source distance at zero, mark it visited and enqueue it. Remove a vertex, then discover its unvisited outgoing neighbours with distance one greater. Mark when enqueuing, not only on dequeue, to prevent repeated queued copies. Inductively, all distance-k vertices are processed before distance-(k+1) vertices, so first discovery gives minimum edge count in an unweighted graph.

sections.title: DFS structure
sections.body: Record a vertex as active on entry and finished on exit. A directed edge to an active ancestor is a back edge and proves a cycle. In an undirected graph, the edge back to the DFS parent is not by itself a cycle. DFS trees depend on start vertex and neighbour order, but reachability does not.

sections.title: Topological order
sections.body: A directed acyclic graph has an ordering putting every edge source before its destination. Reverse DFS finishing order gives one after confirming acyclicity. Alternatively Kahn's algorithm repeatedly removes zero-indegree vertices. If fewer than V vertices are removed, a cycle remains. Multiple valid topological orders may exist.

steps: Enqueue A at distance 0; discover B,C at distance 1.
Processing B discovers D at distance 2; mark it immediately.
Processing C does not reenqueue D. A shortest A-to-D route uses 2 edges.
A and B initially have indegree zero.
Remove them in either order; only then does C become available.
Remove C, then D. A,B,C,D and B,A,C,D are both valid.

pitfalls: BFS edge-count shortest paths do not solve arbitrary weighted paths.
In an undirected DFS, skip the parent edge in cycle detection.
revision: Reverse finish order topologically sorts a DAG.

lessons.title: Minimum spanning trees: cuts, Kruskal and Prim
lessons.prerequisite: Weighted undirected graphs and greedy proofs.
lessons.intuition: An MST connects every vertex with minimum total edge weight and no cycles. It is a global network-design objective. The cut property gives a safe local choice and makes greedy algorithms possible.

sections.title: Cut and cycle properties
sections.body: A cut partitions vertices into two nonempty sets; a crossing edge joins the sides. A lightest crossing edge is safe for some MST compatible with current choices under the standard cut argument. If it is uniquely lightest, it belongs to every MST. A uniquely heaviest edge on a cycle cannot belong to any MST. Equal weights require care: several trees may have equal optimal total weight.

sections.title: Kruskal
sections.body: Sort all edges increasingly. Maintain a disjoint-set structure for chosen components. Add an edge if its endpoints are in different components and union them; otherwise reject the cycle-closing edge. Stop at V−1 chosen edges for connected input. Sorting usually dominates at O(E log E).

sections.title: Prim
sections.body: Start at any vertex and repeatedly pick a cheapest edge connecting the current tree to an outside vertex. Maintain best connection keys using a priority queue. This resembles Dijkstra operationally but keys represent cheapest incident attachment, not full source distance. With a binary heap and adjacency lists, a common bound is O(E log V).

steps: Take AB then BC, connecting A,B,C.

lessons.title: Dijkstra, Bellman–Ford and Floyd–Warshall
lessons.prerequisite: Graph relaxation, heaps and dynamic programming.
lessons.intuition: Shortest-path algorithms differ mainly in how they schedule relaxation and which edge weights their proofs tolerate. Treat unreachable distances as infinity and preserve path predecessors if you need a route rather than just its cost.

sections.title: Dijkstra finalization
sections.body: Initialize source to 0 and others to infinity. Extract the unfinalized minimum tentative distance, then relax its outgoing edges. Nonnegative edges ensure no later route through a farther vertex can improve the finalized vertex. A reachable negative edge breaks that proof. Zero weights are allowed. Binary-heap adjacency-list implementations commonly take O((V+E)log V).

sections.title: Bellman–Ford
sections.body: Relax all edges up to V−1 rounds. After round k, shortest paths using at most k edges have been accounted for in the standard formulation. A simple shortest path uses at most V−1 edges when no reachable negative cycle improves it. Another improving pass identifies a reachable negative cycle; not every negative edge is a negative cycle.

sections.title: Floyd–Warshall
sections.body: Let Dᵏ[i,j] allow internal vertices only from the first k. Transition is min(Dᵏ⁻¹[i,j],Dᵏ⁻¹[i,k]+Dᵏ⁻¹[k,j]). It either avoids k or routes through k. Use k as the outer loop in the ordinary in-place implementation, with O(V³) time and O(V²) storage. Negative diagonal values after completion detect relevant negative cycles.

lessons.title: Finite automata and regular expressions
lessons.intuition: Finite automata remember only which state they are in. A state should summarize exactly the past information needed to decide future acceptance. This viewpoint is more useful than memorizing transition drawings: design the meaning of states before adding edges.

sections.title: DFA and NFA semantics
sections.body: A DFA has a total transition function Q×Σ→Q, one start state and a set of accepting states. Read the entire string before deciding acceptance. An NFA may have multiple possible transitions and epsilon moves; it accepts if at least one complete path ends accepting. Epsilon moves consume no symbol. Both models recognize exactly regular languages.

sections.title: Subset construction
sections.body: A DFA state can represent a set of possible NFA states. Start with the epsilon closure of the NFA start. For a symbol, take all corresponding moves and then epsilon closure again. A subset is accepting if it contains an accepting NFA state. Up to 2ⁿ subsets exist for n NFA states, but many may be unreachable.

sections.title: Expressions and minimization
sections.body: Regular expressions use union, concatenation and Kleene star; star includes the empty string. Precedence usually places star above concatenation above union. To minimize a DFA, remove unreachable states and distinguish accepting from nonaccepting states, then refine classes when transitions lead to different classes. States are equivalent only if no suffix distinguishes their acceptance.

lessons.title: Context-free grammars, derivations and pushdown automata
lessons.intuition: A stack lets a machine remember arbitrarily many pending obligations in last-in-first-out order. Context-free grammars describe recursive structure, and pushdown automata recognize the same language class. Nested parentheses and matched counts are natural examples.

sections.title: Grammar mechanics
sections.body: A CFG has variables, terminals, a start variable and productions whose left side is one variable. Derivation replaces a variable using a production. A leftmost derivation always expands the leftmost variable; rightmost expands the rightmost. A parse tree records hierarchical structure, not the temporal order of independent expansions.

sections.body: A pushdown automaton chooses transitions using the current state, input symbol or epsilon, and stack top. For 0ⁿ1ⁿ, push one marker per 0, then pop one per 1 and accept when input and markers are exhausted. It must prevent returning to the zero phase after ones begin. Nondeterministic PDAs recognize all CFLs; deterministic PDAs recognize a proper subclass.

sections.title: Ambiguity and closure
sections.body: A grammar is ambiguous if some string has two distinct parse trees, equivalently distinct leftmost derivations. A grammar can be changed while preserving its language. lessons.title: Turing machines and undecidability
lessons.prerequisite: Automata, proof by contradiction and algorithms.
lessons.intuition: A Turing machine adds an unbounded writable tape to finite control. It models general algorithmic computation. The crucial distinction is whether a machine always halts with an answer or may run forever on some negative instances.

sections.title: Deciders and recognizers
sections.body: A decider halts on every input and accepts exactly its language. A recognizer accepts members but may reject or loop on nonmembers. Every decidable language is recognizable, but not conversely. If both a language and its complement have recognizers, interleave their steps; one must accept, giving a decider.

sections.title: The halting contradiction
sections.body: Suppose H can decide whether any machine halts on an input. Construct D that on machine code x loops if H says machine x halts on x, and halts otherwise. Running D on its own code makes either prediction contradict what D does. Thus no general halting decider exists.

sections.title: Reductions and Rice
sections.body: To show B undecidable, reduce a known undecidable A to B: transform A instances computably so a hypothetical B decider would decide A. Reversing the reduction proves the wrong implication. Rice’s theorem states every nontrivial property of the language recognized by a machine is undecidable; syntactic facts such as the number of states are not such semantic properties.

Assume a computable transform maps x∈A iff f(x)∈B.
If B had a decider, first compute f(x), then call it and return the same answer.
That would decide A. If A is undecidable, B cannot have such a decider.

Reduction direction is essential.
Rice applies to semantic language properties, not all machine properties.

Known hard A≤B establishes hardness of B.

lessons.title: Lexical analysis and tokenization
lessons.intuition: The lexer groups characters into meaningful token classes before the parser checks grammar structure. A token records a category and possibly an attribute, while the lexeme is the actual source substring. Separating them lets a grammar treat every identifier similarly.

sections.title: Token definitions
sections.body: Identifiers, keywords, numeric literals, operators and punctuation are common token classes. Regular expressions describe many lexical patterns; automata implement them. Whitespace and comments may be discarded or retained as metadata depending on the language. Symbol-table entries link identifier tokens to later declaration/type information.

sections.title: Longest match and priority
sections.body: At each input position, a lexer typically chooses the longest matching lexeme. When matches have equal length, a rule priority resolves the tie, often recognizing a keyword before a generic identifier. Thus >= is one token rather than > followed by = if the token rule allows it. A keyword prefix inside an identifier does not force splitting: whilex can remain an identifier.

sections.title: Errors and boundaries
sections.body: A lexical error is an unrecognized character sequence under the token rules. A valid token sequence can still have a parse error, such as misplaced parentheses. Nested structure is ordinarily handled by the parser, not by ordinary finite-automaton token rules. Scanner buffering must preserve character positions and handle end-of-input correctly.

lessons.title: Parsing, FIRST/FOLLOW and LL/LR methods
lessons.intuition: A parser discovers grammatical structure in a token stream. Predictive parsing chooses productions before seeing their full result; bottom-up parsing recognizes handles after seeing the right-hand side. FIRST and FOLLOW sets summarize where grammar decisions can be made.

sections.title: FIRST and FOLLOW
sections.body: FIRST(α) contains terminals that can begin a string derived from α, plus ε if α can disappear. For a sequence, continue into later symbols when earlier ones are nullable. FOLLOW(A) contains terminals that can follow A in some sentential form; the start symbol includes end marker $. For A→αBβ, add FIRST(β) without ε to FOLLOW(B), and if β is nullable add FOLLOW(A).

sections.title: LL(1) prediction
sections.body: For A→α, put the production under terminals in FIRST(α); if α is nullable, also under FOLLOW(A). A conflict means the grammar is not LL(1) as written. Eliminate direct left recursion and factor common prefixes when appropriate, without assuming those changes fix every grammar. Recursive descent expands a leftmost derivation.

sections.title: Bottom-up parsing
sections.body: An LR parser tracks states representing viable prefixes, shifts input symbols and reduces a recognized right-hand side to its left-hand variable. Reductions reconstruct a rightmost derivation in reverse. Shift/reduce and reduce/reduce conflicts signal ambiguity or insufficient parsing information for the chosen method. LR handles a wider grammar class than LL(1).

lessons.title: Syntax-directed translation and runtime environments
lessons.intuition: A parse tree can carry semantic information such as expression values or types. Syntax-directed translation describes how this information moves. Runtime environments then arrange the storage needed when the translated program actually executes.

sections.title: Attributes and evaluation
sections.body: Synthesized attributes are computed from children and flow upward; inherited attributes receive information from a parent or relevant siblings. Semantic rules define dependencies, and a legal evaluation order respects that dependency graph. S-attributed definitions use only synthesized attributes and fit bottom-up evaluation naturally. L-attributed definitions restrict inherited dependencies for left-to-right evaluation.

sections.title: Translation actions
sections.body: An annotated syntax tree can compute expression types, values, offsets or emitted code. For E→E₁+T, a synthesized value rule may set E.val=E₁.val+T.val. Translation schemes embed actions in productions, so action placement determines execution order during a derivation. Parsing correctness alone does not guarantee the semantic actions are correct.

sections.title: Runtime storage
sections.body: An activation record can include arguments, return address, saved registers, locals and links. A dynamic link points to the caller’s frame; a static link supports lexical nesting and can point somewhere different. Stack allocation supports ordinary call-return lifetimes; heap allocation supports objects that outlive their creating call. Recursion needs separate frames even for the same function.

lessons.prerequisite: Expressions, CFG control flow and sets.
lessons.intuition: Intermediate representations expose simple operations and control flow so optimizations can reason about program behaviour. An optimization must preserve observable semantics; matching expression text is insufficient when operands may have changed.

sections.title: Three-address code and blocks
sections.body: Break compound expressions into assignments with at most a small fixed number of operands, such as t1=b*c; t2=a+t1. A basic block has one entry and no internal control-flow branch except at its end. Leaders include the first instruction, jump targets and instructions following jumps. A control-flow graph connects blocks by possible transfers.

sections.title: Local optimization
sections.body: Constant folding evaluates constant expressions; constant propagation substitutes known constants. Common-subexpression elimination reuses a previously computed expression only if its operands and relevant memory remain unchanged. Dead-code elimination removes computations whose results have no future use, provided they have no required side effects. Overflow, aliasing and floating-point rules can constrain algebraic transformations.

sections.body: Liveness is a backward may-analysis: OUT[B]=union of successors' IN sets; IN[B]=USE[B]∪(OUT[B]−DEF[B]). A variable is live if some continuation reads its current value before redefinition. Available expressions use forward propagation and typically intersection at joins because an expression must be available on every incoming path. Iterate finite-set equations to a fixed point.

name: Operating System
description: Processes, memory and the systems between them

lessons.title: System calls, processes, threads and IPC
lessons.intuition: A running program needs an execution context and protected resources. Processes give resource isolation; threads share much of that context while scheduling independently. Kernel entry is controlled because ordinary programs must not directly manipulate every device or other process.

sections.title: System calls and process states
sections.body: A system call enters privileged kernel handling through an architecture-defined trap mechanism. The kernel validates arguments and performs protected work. A process can be running, ready or blocked; blocked means waiting for an event, not merely waiting for CPU. A context switch saves and restores execution state and is distinct from any user-to-kernel mode transition.

sections.title: Threads and creation
sections.body: Threads in one process share an address space and open resources but normally have separate stacks and register contexts. A process creation mechanism such as fork copies a logical process context; modern implementations may initially share pages via copy-on-write. Different processes do not ordinarily share arbitrary writable memory unless explicitly arranged.

sections.title: IPC mechanisms
sections.body: Pipes and message queues move data with OS coordination. Shared memory lets processes access a common region and can reduce copying but requires synchronization. Signals provide notifications rather than general large-data transfer. Blocking calls suspend a caller until conditions are met; nonblocking calls return immediately with status. Choose the mechanism based on data size, synchronization and isolation needs.

steps: A process waiting for the scheduler after exhausting a time slice is ready.
A process waiting for disk completion is blocked.
When disk completion arrives, it usually becomes ready before the scheduler runs it again.

examples.prompt: Two threads modify a shared global
steps: Both threads refer to the same process-global object.
Each still has its own local stack variables and instruction pointer.
Sharing the global creates a synchronization responsibility; having two stacks does not isolate global state.

pitfalls: A mode switch is not necessarily a process switch.
Shared memory does not automatically synchronize access.
revision: Process isolates resources; threads share address space.
Ready waits for CPU; blocked waits for an event.

checks.explanation: One stack per thread gives four stacks.

checks.prompt: A single CPU runs one thread at an instant in this simplified model. How many threads can be running simultaneously?
checks.hint: Ignore multicore hardware in the stated model.
checks.explanation: A single execution core runs one thread at a time.

Kernel entry is controlled because ordinary programs must not directly manipulate every device or other process.

lessons.title: Concurrency, mutexes and semaphores
lessons.intuition: Concurrency allows operations to overlap in time even on one CPU. If a shared update consists of separate read and write steps, scheduling can interleave those steps and lose information. Correct synchronization constrains interleavings, not just the final line of source code.

sections.title: Race conditions and critical sections
sections.body: A data race involves unsynchronized conflicting accesses under the applicable memory model; broader race conditions make correctness depend on timing. A critical section protects shared invariants. Mutual exclusion ensures at most one entrant, while progress and bounded waiting address liveness. Declaring an object volatile is not a substitute for atomicity or a lock.

sections.title: Mutex and semaphore
sections.body: A mutex gives exclusive ownership around a protected region. A semaphore maintains a count with atomic wait and signal operations. wait decrements when available or blocks; signal returns a permit or wakes a waiter under the implementation model. A binary semaphore can coordinate single access but ownership semantics need not match a mutex. Counting semaphores manage multiple identical resources.

sections.title: Producer–consumer
sections.body: For a capacity-N buffer, use empty=N, full=0 and a mutex for buffer manipulation. Producer waits for empty then locks, inserts, unlocks and signals full; consumer symmetrically waits for full and later signals empty. Waiting for availability while holding the buffer mutex can block the other side from making progress.

examples.prompt: Show a lost update for shared x=0
steps: Thread A reads 0; thread B reads 0.
A computes and stores 1; B also computes and stores 1.
Two increments finish with x=1 rather than 2. Locking the whole read-modify-write operation prevents that interleaving.
Initialize semaphore count to 3.
Three successful waits consume all permits, leaving 0.
A fourth requester must block until some owner signals, restoring a permit.

pitfalls: Protect the whole invariant update, not only one read or store.
Incorrect lock order can introduce deadlock.
revision: Mutual exclusion protects safety; progress/bounded waiting protect liveness.
Counting semaphore permits model resource capacity.

checks.hint: Each successful wait consumes one permit.

checks.prompt: Two correctly locked increments start from x=7. What is the final value?
checks.hint: Both increments take effect serially.

lessons.title: Deadlock, avoidance and safe states
lessons.intuition: Deadlock is a circular dependency in which participants cannot proceed. A state can be unsafe without already being deadlocked: unsafe means future declared resource demands might prevent a guaranteed completion order.

sections.title: Necessary conditions
sections.body: The standard Coffman conditions are mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no forced resource preemption and circular wait. All are necessary in the usual resource-allocation model. Prevention deliberately breaks one, for example imposing a global resource-acquisition order to rule out circular waiting.

sections.title: Avoidance with Banker
sections.body: Each process declares its maximum demand. Need=Max−Allocation, and Available is the currently free vector. A safety test repeatedly finds a process with Need≤Work, assumes it completes, and adds its Allocation back to Work. If all can be removed, the resulting sequence certifies safety. A resource request is tentatively granted only if the new state passes the test.

sections.title: Detection and model limits
sections.body: In a single-instance resource graph, a cycle corresponds to deadlock; with multiple instances, a cycle need not be sufficient. Detection examines actual allocations and outstanding requests rather than maximum future claims. Recovery can terminate or roll back processes or preempt suitable resources. Starvation is indefinite denial to a participant while others may still progress, which differs from deadlock.

examples.prompt: Check safety: Available=1, P1 allocation=1/max=2, P2 allocation=1/max=3
steps: Needs are 1 and 2.
P1 can finish using the available unit, releasing its allocation and making Work=2.
P2 can then finish. Sequence P1,P2 certifies safety.
Every thread must acquire lock A before lock B.
A thread holding B cannot wait for A because that acquisition order is disallowed.
This removes a possible A↔B circular wait, though other correctness concerns still need analysis.

pitfalls: Unsafe is not synonymous with already deadlocked.
A cycle is not sufficient in every multiple-instance resource graph.
revision: Safety test simulates finishing processes and releasing allocations.

checks.prompt: Which statement about an unsafe resource state is correct?
checks.hint: Avoidance reasons about possible future demands.
checks.explanation: Unsafe means no safe sequence under declared maximum demands. Current requests may still permit progress, so actual deadlock is not established.

lessons.title: CPU and I/O scheduling
lessons.intuition: Scheduling chooses which waiting work receives a resource next. A schedule should be traced on a time axis using arrival times and preemption rules. Waiting, response and turnaround times describe different experiences and should not be interchanged.

sections.title: CPU metrics
sections.body: Turnaround=completion−arrival. In the single CPU-burst model, waiting=turnaround−burst. Response time measures first execution−arrival. FCFS serves arrival order and may create a convoy behind a long job. Nonpreemptive SJF picks the shortest available next burst; shortest-remaining-time-first is its preemptive variant. Future arrivals cannot be scheduled before they exist.

sections.title: Round-robin
sections.body: Run each ready process for at most quantum q, then requeue if unfinished. Small q improves opportunities for responsiveness but raises context-switch overhead; very large q approaches FCFS. At simultaneous arrivals/completions define the queue tie convention. Priority scheduling may starve low-priority work; aging can increase priority over time.

sections.title: Disk scheduling
sections.body: FCFS follows request order. SSTF picks the nearest requested cylinder, potentially starving distant requests. SCAN moves in a direction and reverses, while LOOK reverses at the last request rather than physical end. C-SCAN serves one direction with a return movement. Total head travel depends on the initial position, direction and whether endpoint movement counts.

examples.prompt: FCFS with both arrivals at 0 and bursts 3,5
steps: Run P1 from 0 to 3 and P2 from 3 to 8.
Waiting times are 0 and 3; mean=1.5.
Turnaround times are 3 and 8; mean=5.5. The metrics differ despite the same schedule.
Closest is 55, movement 5.
From 55, closest remaining is 80, movement 25.
Finish at 10, movement 70. Total movement=5+25+70=100 cylinders.

pitfalls: Consider only processes that have arrived.
Disk LOOK and SCAN endpoint rules differ.
revision: Waiting=turnaround−burst in the stated CPU-only model.

checks.prompt: Arrival=2, completion=12 and CPU burst=6. What is waiting time?
checks.hint: Compute turnaround first.
checks.explanation: Turnaround=12−2=10; waiting=10−6=4.

checks.hint: Add absolute differences.

lessons.title: Memory management, virtual memory and file systems
lessons.intuition: Virtual memory separates a program’s address space from physical placement. A translation may be missing from the TLB even when the page is resident; a page fault instead means the required resident mapping cannot complete normally and OS handling is needed.

sections.title: Paging and translation
sections.body: Split a virtual address into page number and offset. The page table maps the page number to a physical frame; offset is unchanged. A TLB caches translations, not ordinarily the data itself. Page-table size depends on page count and entry size. Larger pages reduce entry count but can increase internal fragmentation. Segmentation models variable-size logical regions and has different allocation trade-offs.

sections.title: Replacement and faults
sections.body: Demand paging loads pages when first needed or after eviction. FIFO removes the oldest loaded page, LRU the least recently used, and optimal the page whose next use is farthest in the future. Optimal needs future knowledge and is a benchmark. FIFO can exhibit Belady’s anomaly; LRU is a stack algorithm and does not. Too few frames for active working sets can cause thrashing.

sections.title: File organization
sections.body: Directories map names to metadata or file identifiers. Contiguous allocation supports simple sequential/random positioning but complicates growth; linked allocation traverses pointers; indexed allocation stores block pointers in an index structure. Free-space maps, access permissions and crash consistency are separate responsibilities. An inode-like record can point to direct and indirect block addresses.

examples.prompt: Translate virtual address 5000 with 4 KiB pages
steps: Page size=4096; page number=floor(5000/4096)=1.
If page 1 maps to frame 7, physical address=7×4096+904=29576.
1 faults and loads; 2 faults and loads.
The second reference to 1 hits but does not change FIFO age.
3 faults and evicts 1, the oldest loaded page. Total faults=3; LRU would evict 2 instead.

pitfalls: A TLB miss is not automatically a page fault.
FIFO age is load order, not last access.

checks.prompt: A TLB miss implies which conclusion?
checks.hint: TLB entries cache translations.
checks.explanation: A page-table lookup may find a valid resident frame. A TLB miss alone does not mean a page fault.
options: The page is definitely on disk
The translation is not currently found in the TLB; the page may still be resident

checks.prompt: With page size 1024 bytes, what is the offset of virtual address 2500?
checks.hint: Take the remainder modulo page size.

lessons.title: File systems, allocation and free-space management
lessons.intuition: A file system connects human names and byte offsets to physical blocks. File metadata, block allocation and directory structure have different responsibilities. A lookup cost depends on which metadata is cached and which indirection levels must be read.

sections.title: Allocation choices
sections.body: Contiguous allocation stores consecutive blocks and computes block location by start+index, but growth and external fragmentation are challenges. Linked allocation stores the next block address in each block or a separate table; random access requires following links unless indexed metadata helps. Indexed allocation keeps a pointer array or tree so a chosen logical block can be located without reading all previous data blocks.

sections.title: Direct and indirect pointers
sections.body: An inode-style record can have several direct pointers, a pointer to one indirect block of addresses, and further levels. If a block has B bytes and an address occupies a bytes, an indirect block holds B/a pointers ignoring metadata. A double-indirect path can cover (B/a)² data blocks. Access cost includes metadata blocks that are not already cached.

sections.title: Directories and consistency
sections.body: Directory entries connect names to file identifiers; hard links can give multiple names for the same file object while symbolic links contain a path to be resolved. Free-space bitmaps or lists track available blocks. Updates spanning allocation, data and metadata need crash consistency, often via journaling or copy-on-write techniques. File permissions control access independently of block placement.

examples.prompt: Capacity with 10 direct pointers plus one indirect pointer
steps: Use 1024-byte blocks and 4-byte addresses, so indirect capacity=1024/4=256 addresses.
Total reachable data blocks=10+256=266.
Maximum data capacity under this simplified structure=266×1024=272384 bytes, excluding metadata itself.
To reach logical block 4, start at logical block 0.
Follow four next-block links unless a separate cached index supplies the location.
Contiguous allocation computes its address directly; the representation changes cost.

pitfalls: An indirect block is metadata, not an additional file-data block.
Count cached and uncached metadata according to the question.
revision: Pointers per index block=block bytes/pointer bytes.
Directories map names; allocation maps logical data to blocks.

checks.hint: Divide bytes by pointer size.
checks.explanation: 4096/8=512 pointers.

checks.prompt: A file uses 3 data blocks of 1024 bytes. What is allocated data capacity?
checks.hint: Multiply block count by size.
checks.explanation: 3×1024=3072 bytes; actual file length may be smaller.

name: Databases
description: Model, query and protect your data

lessons.title: ER modelling, relational schemas and integrity
lessons.intuition: A database model captures which facts exist and how they relate. ER diagrams express entities and relationships at a conceptual level; relational schemas encode them as tables with keys and constraints that prevent invalid states.

sections.title: ER concepts and mapping
sections.body: Entities have identifying attributes; relationships link entities with cardinality and participation constraints. A one-to-many relationship is often represented by a foreign key on the many side. A many-to-many relationship becomes its own relation with foreign keys to both sides and any relationship attributes. Weak entities require an owner key plus their partial identifier.

sections.title: Relational keys
sections.body: A superkey uniquely determines a tuple; a candidate key is a minimal superkey. Choose one candidate as primary key. Keys can span multiple attributes, and additional unique constraints can express alternate keys. Relations in the mathematical model are sets of tuples, unlike SQL’s default duplicate-preserving query results.

sections.title: Integrity
sections.body: Domain constraints restrict value types/ranges; entity integrity requires primary-key values not be NULL; referential integrity requires a non-NULL foreign key to match an allowed referenced key. Deleting a referenced tuple may be rejected or trigger defined cascading/set-null actions. A foreign key need not be unique on the referencing side.

steps: Student has key student_id; Course has key course_id.
Because many students take many courses, create Enrollment(student_id,course_id,grade).
The pair can be its key if each student takes each course once, and both identifiers are foreign keys. Repeated offerings would need an additional term/attempt attribute.
If student_id alone identifies a row, {student_id,name} also identifies it.
The larger set is a superkey.
It is not a candidate key because removing name still preserves uniqueness.

pitfalls: A candidate key is minimal by inclusion, not simply smallest-looking.
A foreign key is not necessarily a unique identifier.

checks.prompt: A many-to-many Enrollment row uses student_id and course_id as its composite key. How many attributes are in that key?
checks.hint: Count the named key components.
checks.explanation: The pair contains two attributes.

checks.prompt: A relation has 3 candidate keys, and one is selected as primary. How many alternate candidate keys remain?
checks.hint: Remove the selected primary from the count.
checks.explanation: 3−1=2 alternate keys.

lessons.title: Relational algebra, tuple calculus and SQL
lessons.intuition: A query describes a derived relation. Algebra describes operations to produce it, while calculus describes a logical condition on desired tuples. SQL uses related ideas but adds practical semantics for duplicates, NULL and grouping.

sections.title: Algebra and calculus
sections.body: Selection σ filters tuples; projection π keeps named columns and removes duplicates in set-based algebra. Cartesian product pairs every tuple; a join filters combinations by a condition. Union and difference require compatible schemas. Tuple relational calculus uses predicates on tuples; safe/range-restricted expressions ensure finite, domain-independent results.

sections.title: SQL order and joins
sections.body: Conceptually FROM/JOIN establishes sources, WHERE filters rows, GROUP BY forms groups, HAVING filters groups, SELECT chooses expressions, and ORDER BY orders results. An inner join requires a match; an outer join also retains unmatched rows with NULL-filled columns. Filtering an outer-joined table in WHERE can discard the unmatched rows and change the intended semantics.

sections.title: Duplicates, aggregates and NULL
sections.body: SELECT ordinarily keeps duplicates; DISTINCT removes them. COUNT(*) counts rows, while COUNT(column) counts non-NULL values. SUM/AVG ordinarily ignore NULL inputs. Comparisons involving NULL usually yield UNKNOWN; WHERE retains only TRUE. Use IS NULL rather than =NULL. SQL OR/AND follows three-valued logic in such cases.

examples.prompt: Count students per department with at least three students
steps: Group Student rows by dept.
Use SELECT dept, COUNT(*) FROM Student GROUP BY dept HAVING COUNT(*)>=3.
The group filter belongs in HAVING; WHERE cannot directly filter by the completed aggregate count.
There are three rows, so COUNT(*)=3.
Only two have non-NULL column values, so COUNT(value)=2.

pitfalls: Projection in relational algebra eliminates duplicates; SQL SELECT does not by default.
NULL is not an ordinary comparable value.
revision: WHERE filters rows; HAVING filters groups.

checks.prompt: Which SQL clause filters groups after aggregation?
checks.hint: Group predicates require already formed groups.
checks.explanation: HAVING filters groups; WHERE filters source rows before aggregation.

checks.hint: Every tuple pairs with every tuple.
checks.explanation: 3×4=12 pairs.

lessons.title: Functional dependencies and normal forms
lessons.intuition: Normalization controls redundancy caused by dependencies. A dependency is a rule about every valid database state, not a coincidence in one sample table. Begin by computing keys; normal-form tests depend on superkeys and prime attributes.

sections.title: Closure and inference
sections.body: X→Y says equal values on X force equal values on Y. Attribute closure X⁺ starts with X and repeatedly adds RHS attributes whose LHS is already present. If X⁺ contains the whole schema, X is a superkey; remove redundant attributes to test minimality. Armstrong’s reflexivity, augmentation and transitivity support sound dependency inference.

sections.title: 2NF, 3NF and BCNF
sections.body: After atomic-value 1NF, 2NF rules out dependence of a nonprime attribute on a proper subset of a candidate key. In 3NF, every nontrivial X→A has X a superkey or A prime, meaning in some candidate key. BCNF drops the prime-attribute exception and requires every nontrivial determinant to be a superkey. BCNF implies 3NF, but not conversely.

sections.title: Decomposition
sections.body: Lossless join means decomposed relations reconstruct exactly the original valid relation, with no spurious tuples. For a binary decomposition into R1,R2, their intersection determining all of R1 or all of R2 under F⁺ is the usual lossless criterion. Dependency preservation permits checking original dependencies without joining. These are separate properties; a BCNF decomposition can lose dependency preservation.

examples.prompt: Normalize R(A,B,C) with A→B and B→C
steps: A⁺={A,B,C}, so A is a candidate key.
B⁺={B,C}; B is not a superkey, and C is nonprime, so B→C violates 3NF and BCNF.
Decompose into AB and BC. Shared B determines BC, so the binary decomposition is lossless and preserves the given dependencies.

examples.prompt: Compute closure with A→B, BC→D and A→C
steps: Start A⁺={A}.
Add B and C from the two A dependencies.
Now BC is present, so add D. A⁺={A,B,C,D}.

pitfalls: Sample rows do not prove a dependency holds universally.
Lossless and dependency-preserving are different tests.
revision: BCNF: every nontrivial determinant is a superkey.

checks.prompt: What is the BCNF rule for a nontrivial functional dependency X→Y?
checks.hint: BCNF removes the prime-RHS exception from 3NF.
checks.explanation: Every nontrivial determinant must be a superkey. A prime RHS can permit 3NF but does not by itself satisfy BCNF.
options: Y must be the primary key
X must be a single attribute

checks.prompt: How many attributes are in B⁺ for the same dependencies?
checks.hint: A cannot be inferred from B.
checks.explanation: B⁺={B,C}, size 2.

lessons.title: File organization and B/B+ tree indexing
lessons.intuition: An index is an auxiliary route to data, not the data model itself. On-disk indexes use high branching factors to reduce expensive page reads. Equality and range queries can prefer different organizations.

sections.title: File layout
sections.body: Heap files place records in convenient free space and favour insertion without key order. Sorted files favour ordered scans but make insertion maintenance costly. Hash organization targets equality buckets and generally does not preserve ordering. A clustered organization aligns data placement with index order; a secondary index may require scattered data-page fetches.

sections.title: B-tree family
sections.body: B and B+ trees remain balanced and store many separator keys per page. In a common B+ design, internal nodes guide search while data entries are at leaves, which are linked for range scans. Definitions of “order” vary: read whether it means maximum children, maximum keys or minimum occupancy. Splits, redistribution and merges preserve occupancy and balance.

sections.title: Cost reasoning
sections.body: With fanout f and many entries, height grows roughly logarithmically in f. Point search follows one root-to-leaf path; a range search locates its starting leaf then walks linked leaves. Dense indexes have an entry for every relevant key/record convention; sparse indexes have selected entries and ordinarily require ordered data. Include data-page reads separately when an index does not contain the required record.

examples.prompt: Estimate maximum leaves for a B+ tree with 3 levels and fanout 4

examples.prompt: Range query using a B+ index
steps: Search down to the leaf containing the first key at least the lower bound.

pitfalls: B-tree “order” conventions are not universal.

lessons.title: Transactions, serializability and concurrency control
lessons.intuition: Transactions group operations into a unit whose intermediate effects must be controlled. Concurrency can improve throughput, but interleavings must preserve an allowed relationship to serial execution and support recovery when work fails.

sections.title: ACID and anomalies
sections.body: Atomicity gives all-or-nothing effects; consistency preserves declared invariants when transactions themselves are correct; isolation controls interference; durability preserves committed effects after recovery. Lost updates overwrite another transaction’s changes. Dirty reads observe uncommitted writes. Nonrepeatable reads and phantoms involve changing rows or predicate result sets across reads.

sections.title: Conflict serializability
sections.body: Two operations conflict if they are in different transactions, access the same item, and at least one writes. Add Ti→Tj when Ti’s conflicting operation precedes Tj’s. The schedule is conflict serializable iff this precedence graph is acyclic; a topological order gives an equivalent serial ordering. Read-read pairs create no edge. Conflict serializability is stronger than some other semantic notions of serializability.

sections.title: Locks and recovery
sections.body: Two-phase locking first acquires locks, then releases without acquiring new ones. It guarantees conflict serializability under the standard model but can deadlock. Strict variants retain required exclusive locks until commit/abort to prevent cascading effects. Write-ahead logging requires appropriate log records be durable before related dirty data pages are written. Recovery may redo committed work and undo uncommitted work according to its logging scheme.

pitfalls: Read-read overlap does not create a conflict.

lessons.title: Layering, switching and network performance
lessons.intuition: A network separates services into layers so each solves a manageable part of delivery. Packets share infrastructure, while circuits reserve capacity. Delay depends on several physical and queueing effects, so bandwidth and latency are not interchangeable.

sections.title: Layers and encapsulation
sections.body: An application message becomes transport data, then a network packet, then a link frame under common Internet layering. Each layer adds addressing/control information appropriate to its scope. A router forwards network-layer packets; a typical Ethernet switch forwards link-layer frames. End-to-end services and per-link services solve different problems.

sections.title: Switching models
sections.body: Circuit switching reserves a route or channel allocation, potentially with setup overhead and unused reserved capacity. Packet switching shares links among packets and can queue under load. Datagram packets can be routed independently; a virtual circuit establishes logical forwarding state before transfer, typically using a label on subsequent packets. A logical virtual circuit is not necessarily a physically reserved circuit.

sections.title: Delay and throughput
sections.body: Transmission delay=L/R for L bits on rate R; propagation delay=distance/signal speed. Processing and queueing add further delay. Store-and-forward requires a full packet before forwarding in the basic model. Bottleneck link rate constrains sustained throughput. With multiple packets and links, serialization can be pipelined; don’t multiply entire end-to-end latency by packet count automatically.

steps: Convert to bits: 1500×8=12000.

steps: The first packet needs one transmission time on each link, total 2t.

Completion is (N+1)t for two equal links under these assumptions, not 2Nt.

pitfalls: Convert bytes to bits before dividing by bit rate.

lessons.title: Error detection, MAC and Ethernet
lessons.prerequisite: Binary polynomials, frames and shared media.
lessons.intuition: The link layer moves frames over one link and manages its local addressing and error checks. Error detection identifies some corrupt frames; it is not automatically error correction. Shared-medium access rules matter only where senders actually contend for the same medium.

sections.title: Parity, checksums and CRC
sections.body: A parity bit detects any odd number of bit flips but can miss an even number. Internet-style checksums use one’s-complement arithmetic. CRC treats bits as polynomial coefficients over GF(2): addition/subtraction is XOR. Append r zeros for a degree-r generator, divide, and append the r-bit remainder. A receiver divides the received codeword; a nonzero remainder detects an error.

sections.title: Medium access
sections.body: ALOHA transmits with probabilistic contention; carrier-sense protocols listen before transmitting. Classic half-duplex Ethernet uses CSMA/CD, detecting collisions and backing off. The minimum frame time must support collision detection over the collision domain under its physical assumptions. Full-duplex switched Ethernet has separate bidirectional links and does not use collision detection.

sections.title: Ethernet switching
sections.body: MAC addresses identify local link interfaces. A learning switch records the source MAC and ingress port. Known destination addresses are forwarded to the corresponding port; unknown destinations and relevant broadcasts are flooded according to VLAN/topology rules. Routers separate network-layer domains; a link switch does not usually choose routes by IP prefix.

Modern full-duplex Ethernet does not use CSMA/CD.

lessons.title: Distance-vector and link-state routing
lessons.prerequisite: Graphs, shortest paths and link costs.
lessons.intuition: Routers need a distributed way to learn where to send packets. Distance-vector exchanges route estimates with neighbours; link-state distributes topology so each router can compute routes locally. The information each approach shares explains its failure modes.

sections.title: Distance-vector update
sections.body: A router x estimates Dx(y)=minᵥ[c(x,v)+Dv(y)] over neighbours v. Each advertisement supplies a neighbour’s current estimate. Updates may be asynchronous and transient inconsistencies arise when links fail. A destination that becomes unreachable may have increasing estimates passed around, producing count-to-infinity.

sections.title: Mitigations and link-state
sections.body: Split horizon avoids advertising a route back on the interface from which it was learned; poisoned reverse explicitly advertises an infinite metric in that direction. These do not solve every possible loop topology. Link-state routers discover neighbours/costs, flood sequenced link-state advertisements and run Dijkstra on their assembled topology. Sequence numbers and aging prevent stale information from circulating indefinitely.

sections.title: Forwarding versus routing
sections.body: Routing computes and updates the control-plane table; forwarding uses it for individual packets. A next hop need not be the destination itself. Correct convergence is distinct from instantaneous consistency during updates. Compare control traffic, stored knowledge and recovery behaviour rather than assuming one protocol is universally superior.

steps: Neighbour A costs 2 and advertises distance 5; candidate cost is 7.
Neighbour B costs 4 and advertises distance 1; candidate cost is 5.

steps: A previously reaches D directly, while B’s route to D uses A.

Split horizon is not a universal cure for every multi-router loop.
revision: Link-state computes shortest paths from flooded topology.

lessons.title: IPv4, CIDR and network address translation
lessons.intuition: An IPv4 address contains 32 bits. CIDR says how many leading bits define the routing prefix. NAT rewrites selected addresses and ports, often allowing several private hosts to share a public address, but it changes end-to-end addressing assumptions.

sections.title: CIDR arithmetic
sections.body: A /p prefix leaves 32−p varying bits and contains 2^(32−p) total addresses. In conventional multiaccess subnets, network and broadcast addresses are not assignable hosts, giving two fewer; /31 point-to-point and /32 cases require different treatment. Masking an address with the subnet mask gives its network prefix. Block boundaries follow the mask, not arbitrary decimal rounding.

sections.title: Longest-prefix match
sections.body: A packet destination may match several routes. Select the matching route with the largest prefix length, because it identifies the most specific region. The default /0 matches everything but loses to any more-specific match. A route’s prefix need not match a classful address boundary; CIDR replaced that restriction.

sections.title: NAT/PAT
sections.body: Address translation rewrites private/public addresses; port translation distinguishes multiple internal transport sessions sharing an external IP. The device keeps mappings and updates required checksums. Incoming connections need a mapping or explicit forwarding arrangement. NAT is not equivalent to a complete security policy and can complicate protocols embedding addresses in payloads.

The last-octet ranges begin 0,64,128,192; 70 lies in 64–127.
Network is 192.168.1.64, conventional broadcast .127, with hosts .65–.126.
All three cover the destination in this example.
The /24 route has the longest prefix.

Do not subtract two blindly for /31 or /32.

lessons.title: IPv4 fragmentation step by step
lessons.prerequisite: IPv4 headers, byte counts and division.
lessons.intuition: An IP datagram may exceed a link’s maximum transmission unit. Fragmentation divides its payload while preserving enough information to reassemble at the destination. Headers are repeated for every fragment, and offsets locate payload bytes rather than whole datagram bytes.

sections.title: Payload capacity
sections.body: MTU limits the total IP fragment length including its own IP header. With header H, payload capacity is MTU−H. Every nonfinal fragment payload must be a multiple of 8 bytes, so use floor((MTU−H)/8)×8 when creating maximal nonfinal fragments. The final payload may be smaller and need not be an eight-byte multiple.

sections.title: Header interpretation
sections.body: Fragments share the relevant source,destination,protocol and identification association. The fragment offset measures where this payload starts in the original payload, in units of 8 bytes. MF=1 says more fragments follow; MF=0 identifies the final portion, not necessarily a complete unfragmented original. DF forbids fragmentation, so an oversize packet must be handled by failure/feedback under the protocol instead.

sections.title: Reassembly reasoning
sections.body: Add payload lengths to verify the original payload total. Calculate offsets cumulatively from payload, excluding repeated headers. IPv4 permits routers to fragment when allowed; destination reassembly handles the pieces. Loss of one needed fragment prevents normal complete delivery of the original datagram, adding a reason large fragmented packets can be fragile.

examples.prompt: Fragment a 4000-byte datagram with 20-byte header across MTU 1500
steps: Original payload=4000−20=3980; nonfinal payload cap=1480, already divisible by 8.
Payload pieces are 1480,1480,1020; total lengths are 1500,1500,1040.

steps: Original payload=1000; maximum nonfinal payload=600.
Pieces are 600 and 400 bytes.
Offsets are 0 and 75; total fragment lengths are 620 and 420.

pitfalls: Offset units are 8 bytes, not bytes.
Subtract the original header before splitting, then add a header to each fragment.

checks.hint: Offsets use eight-byte units.

checks.explanation: 2020−20=2000 payload bytes.

lessons.title: TCP flow/congestion control, sockets, DNS and HTTP
lessons.intuition: TCP transports an ordered byte stream using sequence numbers, acknowledgments and retransmission. The receiver’s capacity and the network’s capacity are separate limits. Application protocols then interpret those delivered bytes or use other transport mechanisms.

sections.title: Reliability and windows
sections.body: TCP sequence numbers refer to bytes, and cumulative acknowledgments identify the next expected byte under the usual model. A receive window rwnd advertises buffering capacity. A congestion window cwnd estimates what the sender should inject into the network. The usable limit is approximately min(rwnd,cwnd) minus bytes already outstanding, subject to further implementation rules.

sections.title: Congestion control
sections.body: In the classical teaching model, slow start grows cwnd roughly exponentially per RTT until a threshold or loss indication. Congestion avoidance grows more slowly, often about one MSS per RTT. Timeout and duplicate-ACK loss reactions differ across variants; read the specified algorithm. Bandwidth-delay product estimates data needed in flight to keep a path busy; a too-small window limits throughput.

sections.title: Sockets, DNS and HTTP
sections.body: A TCP server commonly socket/bind/listen/accepts; a client connects, then both send/receive a byte stream without preserved message boundaries. DNS maps names and other records through hierarchy and caches, commonly using UDP but also TCP. HTTP defines methods, status codes, headers and message semantics. Persistent connections reuse transport. HTTP/3 runs over QUIC/UDP, so do not assume every HTTP version uses TCP.

steps: rwnd=16000 bytes, cwnd=10000 bytes and outstanding=4000.

lessons.title: The socket API and TCP byte-stream framing
lessons.intuition: A socket is a programming interface to network communication. Establishing a connection and exchanging application messages are separate tasks. TCP delivers a byte stream, so the application must decide how to recognize message boundaries.

sections.title: Server lifecycle
sections.body: Create a socket, bind it to a local address/port, listen for incoming connections and accept. accept returns a connected socket for one peer while the listening socket remains for future connections. A server can serve multiple clients using threads, processes or nonblocking/event-driven I/O. Privileged-port and address-binding rules depend on the OS.

sections.title: Client and data transfer
sections.body: A TCP client creates a socket and calls connect to the server endpoint. send/recv may transfer fewer bytes than requested; robust code loops as needed. A recv returning zero for a TCP stream indicates an orderly peer closure after available data is exhausted. Errors and timeouts need handling rather than assuming every operation completes immediately.

sections.title: Application framing
sections.body: One send call need not equal one recv call. Define a length prefix, delimiter with escaping, fixed record size or another protocol framing scheme. Accumulate incoming bytes until one complete message is available, retain surplus bytes for the next message, and bound lengths to avoid unbounded allocation. Network byte order converts multibyte integer fields consistently.

steps: Encode length 5 in the agreed prefix format.

lessons.title: DNS hierarchy, resolution and caching
lessons.intuition: DNS distributes naming information across a hierarchy rather than storing every name in one central server. Resolution may require several queries, but caching avoids repeating most of that work until records expire.

sections.title: Names and authority
sections.body: A domain name is a sequence of labels. Root servers direct queries toward relevant top-level-domain servers, which direct them toward authoritative servers for delegated zones. An authoritative answer describes data in that zone; a recursive resolver acts for a client and obtains/caches answers. Delegation boundaries and host labels are not interchangeable concepts.

sections.title: Query behaviour
sections.body: In recursive resolution, the requester asks a resolver to return a final answer or failure. The resolver can use iterative queries, following referrals rather than asking each upstream server to do the whole lookup. Cached records have TTL lifetimes. Caching both answers and referrals can reduce later queries; a cached IP may expire before or after related delegation records.

sections.title: Records and transport
sections.body: A records map names to IPv4 addresses; AAAA to IPv6; CNAME expresses aliases; MX identifies mail exchangers; NS identifies name servers. DNS commonly uses UDP port 53 for ordinary queries and can use TCP, including for larger/truncated responses and zone transfers under their relevant rules. DNS is not always UDP, and a domain can map to more than one address.

steps: A client asks its recursive resolver.
The resolver follows root and TLD referrals to a relevant authoritative server.
It returns the answer and caches permitted records for their TTLs; future queries can skip steps if caches are valid.

examples.prompt: A cached record has TTL 120 seconds and was stored 45 seconds ago
steps: Assuming no refresh or eviction, remaining valid lifetime is 75 seconds.
A query before expiry can use the cached record.
After expiry, the resolver must obtain fresh information rather than trusting that TTL indefinitely.

pitfalls: Recursive resolver and authoritative server have different roles.
DNS also uses TCP.

checks.hint: Subtract elapsed time.

checks.hint: Use IPv4 address width.

lessons.title: HTTP requests, responses and persistent connections
lessons.intuition: HTTP defines application-level meaning: which resource is requested, what action is asked for and how the response is described. Its semantics are separate from the transport connection and remain recognizable across protocol versions.

sections.title: Request and response structure
sections.body: A request carries a method, target and headers, often with a body. GET retrieves a representation; POST commonly submits processing data; PUT replaces at a known target under its semantics. A response includes a status code, headers and possibly a body. Status classes 2xx indicate success, 3xx redirection, 4xx client-side request problems and 5xx server-side failures.

sections.title: Persistence and latency
sections.body: Persistent connections reuse transport for multiple requests, reducing repeated setup. HTTP/1.1 generally supports persistent connections; HTTP/2 multiplexes streams within its transport model. HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP rather than TCP. A latency question must specify DNS/cache state, connection establishment, transfer size, request dependencies and whether connections can be reused.

sections.title: Caching and security
sections.body: Cache-Control and related metadata control reuse; conditional requests can validate existing content rather than redownload it. HTTPS protects HTTP exchange using the applicable secure transport, but does not change what GET or a status code means. An HTTP cache and a DNS cache store different information and can have unrelated expiry times.

steps: If each new TCP connection costs one setup RTT, three separate connections pay three setup RTTs in this simplified model.

Two setup RTTs are saved; actual response delays and transfers must still be included.

pitfalls: Connection refusal is not an HTTP error response.
HTTP/3 does not use TCP.

lessons.title: Quantitative aptitude: ratios, percentages and work
lessons.intuition: Quantitative aptitude usually rewards a clean model rather than lengthy computation. Define units and the reference quantity first. A percentage is relative to a base; a work time converts to a rate before people working together can be combined.

sections.title: Ratios and averages
sections.body: If A:B=a:b, write A=ak and B=bk. This preserves the relationship while totals determine k. A weighted average is total weighted value divided by total weight, not the unweighted average of subgroup averages. Check whether group sizes are equal before averaging percentages.

sections.title: Successive changes
sections.body: Increase by p% multiplies by 1+p/100; decrease by q% multiplies by 1−q/100. Combine multipliers to find overall change. Equal percentage rises and falls do not cancel because their bases differ. Profit percentage uses cost price as its base unless explicitly redefined.

sections.title: Work and speed
sections.body: A worker completing one job in t days works at 1/t jobs per day under constant-rate assumptions. Independent rates add for shared work; time is reciprocal total rate. Distance=rate×time with consistent units. Relative speed adds for opposite travel directions and subtracts for same-direction catch-up.

steps: After the rise, value=120.
The reduction is 20% of 120, which is 24.
Final value=96, a 4% overall decrease.

examples.prompt: A finishes in 6 days and B in 3 days
steps: Rates are 1/6 and 1/3 jobs/day.
Combined rate=1/2 job/day.

pitfalls: Percentages of different bases cannot be simply added.
Add work rates, not completion times.

checks.prompt: Two workers each finish a job in 8 days. Together how many days do they need?
checks.hint: Add their equal rates.
checks.explanation: 1/8+1/8=1/4 job/day, so 4 days.

lessons.title: Verbal, analytical and spatial aptitude
lessons.prerequisite: Reading comprehension and careful constraint tracking.
lessons.intuition: Reasoning tasks ask you to respect exactly the available evidence. In verbal problems, grammatical role and meaning constrain the answer; in arrangements, each clue reduces the allowed states. Spatial questions require tracking invariants through transformations rather than guessing from familiarity.

sections.title: Language and comprehension
sections.body: For grammar, identify subject, verb, modifiers and required agreement. Distinguish possession (their), contraction (they’re) and location (there). For passages, separate explicit statements from reasonable but unsupported assumptions. An inference must follow from the passage, not merely be plausible in real life. Analogy questions should preserve the exact relationship, such as increasing intensity or part-to-whole.

sections.title: Analytical constraints
sections.body: Translate clues into explicit relations: before, immediately before, adjacent or not adjacent are different. Draw positions, place fixed clues, then enumerate remaining possibilities systematically. In circular seating, rotationally equivalent arrangements may be treated as the same, but reflection equivalence depends on the question. Use a counterexample arrangement to test whether a claim must always hold.

sections.title: Spatial transformations
sections.body: A rotation preserves orientation/chirality and pairwise distances; a reflection reverses handedness. For cube nets, track which faces become opposite, then rule out options placing opposite faces adjacent. When counting figures, classify by size and position so overlaps are included without counting the same figure twice. Explicit sketches are useful working tools.

examples.prompt: Three positions with A immediately before B and C after B
steps: A,B must occupy adjacent positions in that order.
C must lie to their right, so A,B cannot occupy positions 2,3.
Only A,B,C remains. Replacing “immediately” with “somewhere” would weaken the adjacency requirement.
The noun books needs a possessive determiner.
Their means belonging to them; they’re expands to they are and cannot fill that noun-modifying role.
There describes location. Choose using grammatical function, not sound.

pitfalls: Do not add unstated constraints.
Immediately before differs from before.
A mirror image need not be obtainable by rotation.

checks.hint: Try every location for the A,B pair.
checks.explanation: Only A,B,C satisfies both constraints.

checks.prompt: Four distinct people stand in a line without restrictions. How many arrangements are possible?
checks.hint: Use factorial ordering.
